Argentina boss Scaloni salutes 'inimitable' Messi after maestro's final game. Argentina’s head coach Lionel Scaloni hailed the enduring genius of the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain striker Lionel Messi on Wednesday moments after the 39-year-old played his last game for the national team.

Franco-Japanese duo Kagan and Soai win 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry. The Nobel Prize in chemistry was awarded on Wednesday to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan’s Kenso Soai for unravelling the mystery of why only one of two forms of certain molecules occurs in nature.

Malian army retakes strategic city of Kidal after Tuareg separatists withdraw. The Malian army and its Russian allies entered the strategic northern city of Kidal on Tuesday without resistance after Tuareg separatists announced a tactical withdrawal, five months after government forces were driven out.

‘I became their slave’: Israeli hostage recounts 500 days in Hamas captivity. Omer Shem Tov was abducted by Hamas at the Nova music festival in Israel on 7 October, 2023 and held hostage by the armed Islamist group for 505 days. The 24-year-old has published a book about his time in captivity, entitled Meeting Myself in Hell. RFI spoke to him at his parents' home near Tel Aviv.

African Union to launch continent's first credit rating agency in Mauritius. The African Union is launching the continent’s first credit rating agency on Wednesday, aiming to provide an alternative to the global “big three” by drawing on African expertise and perspectives.

US top diplomat Rubio says West must choose ‘national power’ or decline. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a combative defence of Washington’s right to wield its “national power” in Athens on Wednesday, while urging Europe to “awaken from its long slumber”.

Bad Cop, worse Cop? EU tempers hopes for UN climate summit. After having its hopes dashed for a more ambitious deal last year in Brazil, the European Union is setting its sights low for next month's Cop31 climate summit in Turkey.

EU and China open crunch trade talks in Beijing on hybrid car exports. European Union trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic arrives in Beijing on Thursday for two days of high-stakes talks with China, with Brussels seeking a pilot agreement to curb the surge in Chinese hybrid-car exports and reduce a trade deficit now running at around €1 billion per day.

French students return to streets despite government bid to ease crisis. High school and university students across France launched a fourth straight day of nationwide action on Thursday, after Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised measures to improve conditions in schools but stopped short of announcing immediate changes.

Court of Arbitration for Sport convenes to rule on 2025 AFCON champions. Senegal's legal attempt to recover the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title will on Thursday go before a three-judge panel at the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which will decide whether Morocco should hand it back to the West African nation.

Ethiopian drone strikes hit Eritrean forces in northern Tigray city. Ethiopian drone strikes have targeted Eritrean forces who had reached a northern Tigrayan city, a conflict monitor and witnesses said on Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.

United States accused of exploiting migrant suffering with Africa deportations. The United States is violating international law by deporting migrants to African countries where they have no ties, NGO Human Rights Watch said on Thursday, accusing Washington of using deportation to remote destinations as a deterrent to immigration.

Soupçons de peste en Russie: plusieurs pays s'inquiètent, Moscou dément tout «risque épidémique». Les autorités russes ont affirmé mercredi 7 octobre qu'il n'existait « aucun risque épidémique » en Sibérie après la mort d'une laborantine d'un institut travaillant sur la peste. Le Kremlin dénonce des « fausses informations » alors que les appels à plus de transparence se multiplient, notamment de la part de l'OMS, de l'UE et des États-Unis.

Après 235 jours passés dans l'espace, Sophie Adenot achève une mission de tous les records dans l’ISS. Après huit mois passés en apesanteur, l’astronaute française Sophie Adenot a quitté la Station spatiale internationale, mercredi 7 octobre. La fin d’une mission historique à plus d’un titre.

Crise du logement en Espagne: la retraitée à l'origine de la mobilisation est décédée. La retraitée madrilène dont l'expulsion a déclenché des manifestations monstres contre la crise du logement en Espagne est morte, mercredi 7 octobre. Les principaux syndicats du pays appellent à la mobilisation générale, alors qu'approchent les élections anticipées convoquées par Pedro Sanchez.

«Nous mangeons comme des oiseaux»: en Italie, les prix alimentaires sévèrement touchés par l'inflation. Face à la hausse vertigineuse de l’inflation qui a atteint 4,2% sur un an, le gouvernement de Giorgia Meloni a demandé à la Commission européenne d’insérer la question de la pression inflationniste dans le Conseil de l’Ecofin du 9 octobre. L’objectif est d’obtenir une flexibilité budgétaire supplémentaire pour aider les entreprises et les ménages.

Mobilisations lycéennes en France: les futurs professeurs de l'Inspé rejoignent le mouvement. Alors que le mouvement des lycéens continue à gagner de nombreux établissements au-delà du secondaire, l'Institut national supérieur du professorat et de l'éducation (Inspé) a été bloqué pour la première fois, mercredi 7 octobre. Une mobilisation spontanée d'une quinzaine de personnes a finalement attiré plus d'une soixantaine de manifestants.

Trois ans après le 7-Octobre, l’agonie se poursuit dans la bande de Gaza. Plus de mille jours après le début de la guerre, la bande de Gaza compte encore ses tués et ses morts. Depuis le soi-disant cessez-le-feu et le plan de paix, l’étau d’Israël sur l’enclave paupérisée ne désarme pas : le blocus n’est pas levé et la libre circulation entravée.

Face à l'écrasante puissance commerciale chinoise, l'Europe cherche la riposte. Le commissaire européen au Commerce, Maros Sefcovic, entame ce jeudi 8 octobre une visite cruciale de deux jours en Chine pour tenter de rééquilibrer les relations commerciales entre les deux blocs. Alors que Paris et Berlin appellent Bruxelles à durcir sa politique commerciale, Pékin met en garde contre toute dérive protectionniste.

Finale de la CAN 2025: «Si vous avez accepté de jouer, vous devrez accepter le résultat qui en découle». Maroc ou Sénégal, qui va être déclaré vainqueur de la dernière Coupe d'Afrique des nations de football qui s'est jouée en janvier dernier ? C'est tout l'enjeu de la réunion à huis clos du Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS), ce jeudi 8 octobre à Lausanne, en Suisse. Aucune décision ne sera rendue dès aujourd'hui, mais les deux pays vont plaider devant le tribunal. Joseph-Antoine Bell a été un grand international camerounais. Il est aujourd'hui consultant pour RFI et expert auprès de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF).

Nouvelle coupe drastique et nouvelle stratégie pour l'aide française au développement. Le projet de loi de finances français acte une nouvelle fois une baisse drastique de l'aide publique au développement. Dans la recherche de 54 milliards d'euros d'économies, les budgets de l'aide ne sont pas épargnés. Près de deux milliards d'euros de moins pour 2027, soit -43 % par rapport à 2026. Le nouveau directeur de l'Agence française de développement était entendu ce 7 octobre à l'Assemblée nationale pour défendre la politique de solidarité internationale.

L'Union africaine lance une agence de notation pour renforcer la souveraineté financière du continent. L’Afrique se dote d’un nouvel outil pour avoir son mot à dire sur les marchés financiers. L’Agence africaine de notation de crédit a été officiellement lancée mercredi 7 octobre à Maurice, avec l’ambition de proposer une lecture africaine du risque financier. L’enjeu est majeur : le coût auquel les États et les entreprises du continent accèdent aux financements. Pour ses promoteurs, une meilleure prise en compte des réalités économiques africaines pourrait contribuer à attirer davantage de capitaux vers le continent. Reste à établir sa crédibilité.

Au lendemain d'attaques meurtrières sur les aéroports saoudiens, les Houthis annoncent de nouvelles frappes. Trois personnes ont été tuées et 36 autres blessées mercredi 7 octobre dans des attaques revendiquées par les Houthis contre des aéroports saoudiens. Riyad promet des représailles contre les rebelles yéménites, soutenus par l'Iran, alors que les combats s'intensifient au Yémen, où plus de 200 000 personnes ont été déplacées depuis la reprise des hostilités en juillet.

DIRECT - Mobilisation des lycéens en France: le gouvernement promet un «plan d'urgence» imminent pour remplacer les enseignants absents. Après la forte mobilisation mardi 6 octobre pour demander plus de moyens, les lycéens et étudiants français sont de nouveau appelés à manifester ce jeudi 8 octobre, pour l'« acte IV » du mouvement. De son côté, le gouvernement multiplie les signes d'apaisement pour mettre fin à la crise. Selon le ministère de l'Éducation nationale, 224 établissements restent totalement fermés ce jeudi, et 151 partiellement.

Vladimir Kara-Mourza: «En Russie, c'est un délit criminel de s'opposer à la guerre en Ukraine». Vladimir Kara-Mourza, opposant russe en exil, ancien prisonnier politique, vice-président de la Fondation Russie Libre est l'invité de RFI ce 8 octobre 2026. De passage à Paris, il commente l'intensification des frappes russes contre l'Ukraine, la situation des prisonniers politiques et les menaces sur les opposants.

Éthiopie: des troupes érythréennes se déploient dans le nord du Tigré. L’implication de l’Érythrée dans le conflit qui déchire l'Éthiopie depuis quinze jours est de plus en plus visible. D’après de nombreux observateurs, des soldats se déploient actuellement sur le territoire du Tigré, dans le nord éthiopien, dans plusieurs localités. Une présence qui fait craindre le retour d’une guerre à grande échelle entre Addis-Abeba et Asmara : les deux pays, à couteaux tirés, ont rompu leurs relations diplomatiques la semaine précédente.

Marco Rubio en Grèce pour secouer des Européens pris en étau. Le secrétaire d'État américain Marco Rubio était à Athènes mercredi 7 octobre. Au programme, une rencontre avec les dirigeants conservateurs grecs, mais surtout un discours pour réveiller, pour secouer l'Europe, dans un lieu historique et symbolique.

Margaret Hamilton, la scientifique américaine derrière le programme informatique d'Apollo, est morte. L'ingénieure et informaticienne américaine Margaret Hamilton est décédée le 30 septembre dernier à l'âge de 90 ans, a fait savoir le Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), où elle a travaillé près de vingt ans. Figure incontournable de la conquête spatiale grâce à l'élaboration du système informatique utilisé par le programme lunaire Apollo, elle a permis aux Américains de battre les Russes lors de la première course à la Lune dans les années 1960-1970.

«Sauver des vies en ne les risquant pas»: en Ukraine, des drones terrestres en première ligne. Théâtre d'une guerre à grande échelle avec la Russie depuis bientôt cinq ans, l'Ukraine devient un lieu privilégié pour les innovations militaires. C'est d'abord en Ukraine que les drones se sont imposés comme le nouvel alpha et oméga du champ de bataille. Russes et Ukrainiens s'appuient aussi sur les véhicules terrestres sans pilote (VTSP). Reportage dans un atelier et une base d'entraînement secrets de « Spartan », la 3e brigade de la garde nationale ukrainienne.

Ukraine: au moins 30 morts dans des frappes russes contre deux bus à Kramatorsk, Kiev également touchée. Les images, postées en ligne par la ​police, montrent des véhicules en feu et des corps gisant au sol, à Kramatorsk, verrou stratégique des forces ukrainiennes dans le Donbass. Au moins trente personnes ont été tuées dans une frappe russe qui a touché deux bus circulant dans la même rue, dix-huit personnes ont aussi été blessées. La capitale a également été visée avec un premier bilan de trois morts.

Au Liban, 82% des ménages peinent à subvenir à leurs besoins essentiels. Depuis le déclenchement de la crise économique et financière en 2019, l’une des plus graves au monde depuis un siècle et demi selon la Banque mondiale, le Liban n’a connu aucun répit. Le pays du cèdre enchaîne tragédie, avec l’explosion du port de Beyrouth en août 2020, instabilité politique, troubles sociaux et guerres. Les données recueillies et analysées par trois agences des Nations unies ces derniers mois montrent que la situation des ménages s’est dégradée à tous les niveaux, surtout depuis la dernière guerre qui a éclaté le 2 mars.

Le prix Nobel de littérature décerné à la Canadienne Anne Carson. Quand elle a appris ce midi la bonne nouvelle, Anne Carson était en Islande, « listening to the wind », « écouter le vent ». 76 ans, l’écrivaine canadienne et grande spécialiste de la poésie grecque a remporté ce jeudi 8 octobre le prix Nobel de littérature. L’Académie suédoise a loué la capacité de son œuvre « à faire dialogue l’Antiquité avec le monde contemporain ».

Italie: le Parlement approuve une réforme électorale contestée mais défendue par Giorgia Meloni. Ce jeudi 8 octobre 2026, les députés italiens ont approuvé une réforme de la loi électorale pourtant décriée par les partis d'opposition. Ceux-ci dénoncent un texte taillé sur mesure par la Première ministre Giorgia Meloni afin de faciliter sa réélection en 2027.

Les députés européens adoptent une résolution pour lutter contre l'entrisme islamiste. Les eurodéputés ont appelé jeudi 8 octobre à une stratégie européenne de lutte contre l'entrisme islamiste et l'influence des Frères musulmans, qui doit en particulier garantir de ne pas financer des associations affiliées. Le Parlement a adopté une résolution en ce sens du groupe PPE (droite) par 381 voix pour, 167 contre et 15 abstentions, lors de la session plénière à Strasbourg. Une initiative très marquée politiquement en pleine campagne présidentielle en France.

Après trois ans de guerre israélienne, y a-t-il de l'eau potable à Gaza?. Boire de l'eau, c'est vital, mais c'est aussi dangereux dans la bande de Gaza. Aux pollutions agricoles et à la salinisation de la nappe phréatique est venue s'ajouter la pollution chimique des bombes de l'armée israélienne et la destruction des infrastructures hydrauliques.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Thames Valley Police agreed warrants to raid two properties were unlawful. A High Court judge has said Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Thames Valley Police have agreed that search warrants that allowed officers to raid two of his properties earlier this year were unlawful.

British consulate in Jerusalem to become 'UK Mission' as diplomats leave. The UK government said it will retain its presence in East Jerusalem as Israel insisted the British consulate in the city had "ceased to function".

Royal Navy serviceman accused of plotting to leak intelligence to Russia appears in court. A junior Royal Navy serviceman accused of plotting to leak classified information to Russia has appeared in court.

Number of wildfires recorded in England in 2026 was second highest on record. England's very hot summer fuelled the second-highest number of wildfires on recent record, according to provisional government figures.
One dead in Poland's second school attack in two days. A school employee was killed and two others were injured after a knife attack in Poland - the second such incident in the country in two days
Man shot dead at memorial service gathering is named. A 40-year-old man shot dead as people gathered for a memorial service in west London on Friday has been named.
Sisters pulled from sea near Brighton took own lives, coroner rules. Three sisters whose bodies were recovered from the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled.

NHS waiting list at its worst since 2025, figures reveal. The waiting list for hospital treatment in England is at its worst since 2025, new figures show, despite record levels of care being delivered.

Nobelpreis für Literatur geht an kanadische Autorin Anne Carson. Schon in der Vergangenheit galt die kanadische Autorin als Favorit auf den Preis. Die 74-Jährige wird nach Angaben der Schwedischen Akademie für ihr „kühnes und einfallsreiches Gesamtwerk“ mit verspielten Dialogen in klassischer Tradition geehrt.

Das Drama vom übersteuerten Leben. Schlaflos in Sausalito: Thomas Ostermeier inszeniert an der Berliner Schaubühne David Adjmis Broadway-Hit „Stereophonic“ mit der Musik von Will Butler. Der tragikomische Held ist der Toningenieur.

Koalition mit der Linken? – „Ich halte das für völligen Wahnsinn“. SPD und Grüne haben sich in Berlin auf Antisemitismus-Regeln für ein mögliches Bündnis mit der Linken verständigt. Kolumnist Christoph Lemmer warnt davor, dass Judenhass damit lediglich formalisiert werde, statt dessen gesellschaftliche Ursachen anzugehen.

„Wir haben einen Rechtsstaat, der seine Zähne verloren hat“. Extremismusexperte Ahmad Mansour wirft der Politik mangelnde Rückendeckung für die Polizei bei Demonstrationen vor. Den Umgang von SPD, Grünen und Linken mit Antisemitismus bei den Berliner Vorgesprächen bezeichnet er als Verrat an der historischen Verantwortung.

Satire gegen Linke und Grüne? Internes Papier soll Pläne für ZDF-Show von Florian Schroeder verraten. Peter Thiel, Alice Weidel und Ulf Poschardt als Talkgäste, dazu ein kritischer Blick auf NGOs: Die neue ZDF-Satiresendung von Florian Schroeder soll sich laut einem Medienbericht gezielt gegen das links-grüne Milieu positionieren.

„Ich will, dass es da knallt und kracht“ – Banaszak und Lanz geraten in Linke-Debatte aneinander. Brandmauer gegen die AfD, Gespräche mit der Linken – bei „Markus Lanz“ muss Felix Banaszak seine Partei gegen den Vorwurf der Doppelmoral verteidigen. Beide fallen sich immer wieder ins Wort.

„Trotz leichter Übergewichtung auf der Aktienseite sehen wir Anleihen zunehmend positiv“. Kapitalmarktstratege Tilmann Galler blickt zusammen mit Dietmar Deffner auf das vierte Quartal an den Kapitalmärkten: „Ein Aufbau von Anleihenpositionen kann helfen, eventuelle Risiken im Technologiezyklus abzudecken.“

Zootierarzt begeistert über seltenen Leoparden-Nachwuchs in Hamburg. Drei Nordchinesische Leoparden sind im Tierpark Hagenbeck geboren worden. Mit ihrer ersten Präsentation nahm der Zoo auch ein neues Gehege für die Elterntiere in Betrieb.

Der Literaturnobelpreis geht an die nordamerikanische Sappho. Oft zeichnet der Literaturnobelpreis Mittelmaß aus, diesmal ist er eine Trophäe für abweichendes Verhalten. Denn die kanadische Dichterin Anne Carson ist eine klassisch gebildete Eigenbrötlerin.

Linke, Grüne und SPD beschließen Sondierungen – Lesen Sie die Antisemitismus-Erklärung im Wortlaut. Linke, Grüne und SPD treten in Berlin in Sondierungen. Vor den Gesprächen einigten sich die Parteien auf Regeln gegen Antisemitismus. Das steht in der „Berliner Vereinbarung“.

„Hier ist ein Irrer, der zerlegt das Auto“, funkte der Team-Manager über Schumacher. Er wurde vom Kiesgruben-Bengel zum besten Rennfahrer der Welt, hat den Deutschen strahlende Rennfahr-Momente beschert. Michael Schumacher ist ein Kunstwerk. Wäre da nur nicht jener Moment gewesen, der alles veränderte.

„Wir wollen die Lanze für Unternehmertum brechen“. Pioneer-Academy-Herausgeber Christoph Keese stellt das Filmprojekt „Wohlstand für alle. Für heute“ über erfolgreiche Unternehmer vor: „Das sind Menschen, die mit Begeisterung, mit technischem Talent, mit Zuversicht, mit Leidenschaft etwas aufgebaut haben.“

„Hier stehen drei demokratische Parteien“ – Linke, Grüne und SPD beschließen Sondierungen. Linke, Grüne und SPD in Berlin nehmen Sondierungsgespräche zur Regierungsbildung auf. Das teilten die drei Parteien zweieinhalb Wochen nach der Wahl zum Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus mit. Sehen Sie hier das Statement der Parteispitzen.

Der Bund wird vier weitere Fregatten bei TKMS bestellen. Nach der Freigabe durch den Haushaltsausschuss des Bundestages soll die Kieler Werft nun insgesamt acht der Kampfschiffe des Typs Meko A-200 für die Deutsche Marine bauen. Sie dienen als Ersatz für das im Sommer gescheiterte Großprojekt der Fregatten F126.

„Ich habe große Bauchschmerzen im Hinblick auf den Landesverband der Linken in Berlin“. SPD-Fraktionsgeschäftsführer Dirk Wiese äußert deutliche Vorbehalte gegen eine Zusammenarbeit mit der Linkspartei in Berlin: „Ich erwarte hier ganz klar eine Distanzierung vom Antisemitismus.“

اقتصاد غزة يتكبد خسائر فادحة بعد 3 سنوات من الحرب. خلفت الحرب على غزة خسائر فادحة في مختلف القطاعات الاقتصادية، وأدت إلى تراجع حاد في النشاط الاقتصادي، فيما تكشف الأرقام حجم الضرر الذي لحق باقتصاد القطاع.
صحفيو غزة يواصلون التغطية وسط مخاطر وتحديات صعبة. يواصل الصحفيون في غزة عملهم تحت القصف، حاملين كاميراتهم في مواجهة الخطر؛ لتوثيق حرب أودت بحياة مئات الصحفيين ودمرت مقارهم ومعداتهم.

من كرتون المساعدات.. فلسطيني يصنع أرجوحة البهجة في غزة. بما تيسر من أدوات يحاول أهالي قطاع غزة أمثال كارم سلمي توفير ألعاب لأطفالهم الذين أفقدتهم الحرب كل شيء، ألعابهم وأجسادهم وحتى مساحة الفرح ضيقتها عليهم، حيث عمد الرجل إلى صنع أرجوحة لطفلته من الكرتون.

مساعد وزير الدفاع اليمني يكشف للجزيرة نت مسار الحرب. أكد اللواء سمير الصبري مساعد وزير الدفاع اليمني -للجزيرة نت- أن الهدف النهائي من المعركة الحالية هو حسم عسكري ينهي سيطرة الحوثيين ويعيد مؤسسات الدولة التي "انقلبوا عليها في عام 2014".

هل يصبح القمر مقبرة للصواريخ؟ مخاوف على مواقع أبولو التاريخية. بعد أكثر من نصف قرن على أولى خطوات البشر فوق القمر، يواجه هذا الإرث التاريخي تهديدا غير متوقع، مع تصاعد سباق فضائي قد يمحو شواهد لا يمكن تعويضها.

"قراراتي مرتبطة باحتمال تجدُّد القتال": ماذا يعني أن تُصبح الحرب "الوضع الطبيعي"؟. كيف تتغير الحياة عندما تطول الحرب إلى حد تصبح فيه تفاصيلها اليومية أمراً مألوفاً؟ من غزة والسودان إلى سوريا ولبنان وليبيا، تحكي شهادات أشخاص لبي بي سي، عاشوا الحروب والنزوح عن عالم تغيّر فيه معنى البيت والأمان والعمل والأسرة والمستقبل، وأصبح التخطيط للحياة مرتبطاً دائماً باحتمال عودة القتال.

حبس فريق صحفي كامل يعيد ملف حرية الصحافة في مصر إلى الواجهة محلياً ودولياً. ألقت وزارة الداخلية المصرية القبض على ستة صحفيين، يعتقد أنهم كامل فريق عمل منصة للتحقق من المعلومات والأخبار عبر تطبيقات التواصل الاجتماعي، على خلفية اتهامهم بنشر أخبار مفبركة ومغلوطة وانتمائهم لجماعة الإخوان المسلمين، المصنفة إرهابية في مصر، في حين نفت "متصدقش" هذه الاتهامات عبر بيان نشرته الخميس، وقالت إن أرشيفها يتضمن مئات التصحيحات لمعلومات نشرتها جهات وشخصيات محسوبة على جماعة الإخوان.

ما الذي ينتظر الشباب العائدين بعد الحرب؟. قد تتوقف الحرب، لكن طريق العودة لا يبدأ بالضرورة مع توقف القتال. فكيف يمكن استعادة حياة تركتها خلفك؟ وماذا تعني العودة إلى منزلٍ مدمر، أو أرض ما زالت مهددة بمخلفات الحرب؟

هل تدخل الإمارات وبريطانيا في أزمة بسبب نادي مانشستر سيتي؟. تقارير تفيد بأن الإمارات العربية المتحدة قد توقف خطط استثمارية على مستوى المملكة المتحدة بقيمة مليارات الجنيهات نتيجة لقرار الدوري الإنجليزي الممتاز.

هل تستغني السعودية عن شراكتها مع الولايات المتحدة؟. لم تعد فكرة تنويع السعودية لشراكاتها الأمنية مجرد حديث عن المستقبل. ففي الخامس من أكتوبر/تشرين الأول، أعلنت السعودية وتركيا وباكستان الانتقال الفوري إلى التنفيذ العملي لالتزامات الدفاع المشترك ضمن "حلف مكة"، واتخاذ الإجراءات اللازمة لتوفير القوات والقدرات العسكرية المتفق عليها وسرعة نشرها في السعودية، إثر استهدافات متكررة للدولة الخليجية من قبل جماعة أنصار الله الحوثي في اليمن.

ماريا فالتورتا: لغز امرأة أعادت كتابة حياة المسيح والعذراء مريم والإنجيل بـ "رؤى خارقة للطبيعة". في عزلتها الطويلة بسبب المرض، روت ماريا فالتورتا مشاهد تفصيلية لم تذكرها الأناجيل المعتمدة عن حياة المسيح وبيئته عن طريق "رؤى وإملاءات" من المسيح نفسه، بحسب تعبيرها، لتصبح إحدى أكثر الشخصيات جدلاً في الكتابات المسيحية الحديثة.

"ألمانيا تواجه أزمة وجودية ومشكلة خطيرة في أجهزتها الاستخباراتية" -في التلغراف. تتناول جولة الصحافة مقالاً عما وصفه بمرور ألمانيا بـ "أزمة وجودية" بعد الاشتباه ببيع الرئيس السابق لجهاز الاستخبارات الخارجية الألماني لمعلومات سرية إلى جهاز استخباراتي أجنبي، وآخر يتناقش أسباباً دفعت طلبة في فرنسا إلى الاحتجاج بسبب ما يعتبر نظاماً تعليمياً "مرهقاً"، ومقالاً ثالثاً عن سلحفاة مسنة تلهم باحثين للبحث عن أسرار طول العمر.

Le port de Dakar peut-il garder son avance face à la concurrence régionale ?. À peine installé à la direction du Port autonome de Dakar (PAD), Doune Pathé Mbengue donne le ton. Modernisation, numérisation, connexion aux réseaux routier et ferroviaire… Face à Abidjan notamment, Dakar a fort à faire pour conserver son rang de port à conteneurs le plus performant d’Afrique subsaharienne.

Niger : disparu depuis août, le journaliste Moussa Kaka est « détenu » par les autorités. La junte menée par Abdourahamane Tiani reprocherait au directeur de la chaîne RTS, et ancien correspondant de RFI, d’avoir « commis une infraction », sans préciser laquelle, et a annoncé qu’il devrait « répondre devant les juridictions ».

Minerais critiques : la RDC mise sur la cartographie de son sous-sol pour séduire les investisseurs. Dans un contexte de transition énergétique et de lutte d’influence entre la Chine et les États-Unis, Kinshasa veut mieux connaître l’étendue de la richesse de son sous-sol en minerais critiques. Un prérequis pour « mieux défendre les intérêts du pays ».

Mohamed Rabie Khlie, le patron de l’ONCF chargé de mettre le Maroc sur les rails du Mondial 2030. Sous la houlette de l’ingénieur de 63 ans, l’Office national des chemins de fer a réussi à moderniser et à étendre le réseau ferroviaire du royaume. Mais au prix d’un équilibre financier précaire et de retards dans sa mue en société anonyme.

Affaire Kemi Seba : la justice sud-africaine rouvre la voie à une extradition vers le Bénin. Incarcéré en Afrique du Sud, l’activiste visé par une extradition vers le Bénin s’est vu refuser la protection diplomatique. Un revers majeur pour sa défense, qui mise désormais sur l’audience prévue en novembre.

Loi anticorruption en RDC : Guillaume Ngefa a-t-il les moyens de ses ambitions ?. Présenté le 28 septembre à l’Assemblée nationale, le projet de loi porté par le ministre de la Justice promet de moderniser la lutte contre la corruption. Reste à savoir s’il pourra réussir dans un domaine où son prédécesseur avait lui-même promis d’agir.

Pourquoi la vente d’Oragroup est devenue une course contre la montre vitale. En quête d’une recapitalisation cruciale, le groupe bancaire panafricain a réuni son conseil d’administration le 7 octobre. En vente depuis 2019, la banque est contrainte de réduire ses octrois de crédits pour assurer sa survie.

Prétoires, pouvoir et réseaux : ces avocats qui façonnent la politique ivoirienne. Habiba Touré, Jean-Chrysostome Blessy, Abdoulaye Meïté… En Côte d’Ivoire, les robes noires s’imposent au premier rang des batailles de partis, au sein desquels ils sont militants ou responsables. Le Palais de justice d’Abidjan est ainsi devenu le nouveau théâtre des luttes de pouvoir.

Présidentielle au Cameroun : quand Anicet Ekane attendait Issa Tchiroma Bakary à Yaoundé. En octobre 2025, l’activiste aujourd’hui décédé a été l’un des principaux soutiens du candidat à la présidentielle. Pourtant, leur alliance face à Paul Biya ne s’est pas déroulée comme prévu.

L’Égypte parviendra-t-elle à contenir l’Éthiopie ?. Le Caire tente de rassembler autour de lui les adversaires de l’Éthiopie, mais on ignore encore quelle est la solidité de l’alliance qu’il a nouée avec l’Érythrée, le Soudan et la Somalie, et quelle sera la réaction de Washington.

Hôtellerie : au Sahel, les acteurs se réinventent sans les ONG ni la clientèle étrangère. Privés d’une partie de leur clientèle internationale par la crise sécuritaire et le recul de l’aide au développement, les hôtels sahéliens repensent leurs offres. De Bamako à Ouagadougou, ils tentent de séduire la clientèle locale.

« C’est le moment de rendre les armes » : à Bissau, le général N’Tam lance un appel aux militaires restés proches d’Embaló. Après l’annonce de la candidature à la présidentielle du président déchu Umaro Sissoco Embaló, se sont ensuivies des rumeurs de mécontentement au sein de la garde présidentielle. Dans la foulée, plusieurs éléments ont été désarmés et placés sous contrôle de l’état-major.

Burkina Faso : 10 choses à savoir sur le général Diaouari, le maître à penser sécuritaire d’Ibrahim Traoré. Très proche du président burkinabè, qui l’a élevé au rang de général en juillet dernier, cet officier au profil de technocrate est devenu central dans le dispositif d’Ibrahim Traoré. Des questions sécuritaires à la communication, en passant par la mise en œuvre du souverainisme économique, il est l’un des stratèges de la junte.

Sénégal : le calendrier de la restructuration de la dette est-il crédible ?. Dakar vise un premier soutien du FMI dès le mois de novembre avant de boucler un accord sur sa dette avec les créanciers en décembre. Mais le calendrier semble particulièrement serré.

Comment la FIFA a contourné son règlement pour favoriser la qualification de la République démocratique du Congo à la Coupe du monde 2026. Selon des documents internes dont « Le Monde » a pris connaissance, l’instance présidée par Gianni Infantino n’a appliqué aucune sanction après l’alignement d’un joueur congolais inéligible lors de plusieurs matchs qualificatifs pour le Mondial, passant outre son propre code de discipline, la jurisprudence et les recommandations de ses juristes.

Dakar : les images des inondations qui frappent la capitale sénégalaise. Une femme et son fils sont morts dans l’inondation de leur maison, selon un témoin. Le président, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, fait état de « pertes en vies humaines ».

Ebola : le Kenya annonce une première mort liée au virus sur son territoire. Le ministre de la santé a déclaré qu’un citoyen kényan, qui est arrivé samedi dans le pays en provenance de la République démocratique du Congo via l’Ouganda, avait été placé en isolement à l’hôpital de Nairobi, avant d’y mourir lundi soir.

Les économies africaines résistent mieux que prévu aux turbulences au Moyen-Orient. La Banque mondiale a augmenté ses prévisions de croissance pour l’Afrique subsaharienne de 4,1 % à 4,3 % en 2026. Les pays qui enregistrent ces bons résultats sont ceux qui exportent du pétrole et des matières premières.

Denis Mukwege et Zeid Ra’ad Al-Hussein : « La République démocratique du Congo doit engager un véritable processus de justice transitionnelle ». Trente ans après le début de la guerre en RDC, les deux figures de la paix appellent, dans une tribune au « Monde », à la création d’un tribunal international spécial pour le Congo, pour en finir avec l’impunité et la répétition des violences.

Au MK2 Bibliothèque, à Paris, le cinéaste franco-sénégalais Alain Gomis et ses petites lumières. Le Centre Pompidou, fermé pour travaux, organise hors les murs une rétrospective de l’œuvre sensorielle du scénariste et réalisateur du 7 au 20 octobre.

Ebola : le Kenya confirme son tout premier mort. Un Kényan vivant en République démocratique du Congo est mort de la maladie à virus Ebola, lundi 5 octobre, dans un hôpital de Nairobi, a annoncé le ministre de la santé kényan. Il s’agit du premier décès lié à cette maladie jamais recensé dans ce pays d’Afrique de l’Est.

Cheikh Hamidou Kane, écrivain et acteur de la construction d’un Sénégal indépendant, est mort. Ecrivain mais aussi homme d’Etat, plusieurs fois ministre, il était à la fois témoin et acteur de l’histoire contemporaine du Sénégal. Cheikh Hamidou Kane est mort le 3 octobre à Dakar, à l’âge de 98 ans.

Génocide des Tutsi au Rwanda : « Le non-lieu à l’encontre des militaires français à Bisesero n’a pas de valeur historique ». La Cour de cassation a définitivement confirmé, début septembre, le non-lieu prononcé en appel à l’égard de cinq militaires français jugés pour « complicité de génocide » au Rwanda en 1994. L’historien Vincent Duclert revient, dans un entretien au « Monde », sur cette décision.

Au Sénégal, les promesses non tenues de l’exploitation pétrolière et gazière. Le pays a découvert des gisements prometteurs en 2014, mais les investissements étrangers n’ont pas suffi à apporter des bénéfices importants. Deux contrats récemment signés témoignent d’une reprise des projets, au ralenti ces dernières années.

Dans la Somalie en guerre, une aide humanitaire empêchée, des populations menacées de famine. Les violents combats entre factions gouvernementales rivales aggravent encore la crise alimentaire qui touche près de sept millions de Somaliens. Fuyant la sécheresse et la faim, les réfugiés ne cessent d’affluer dans les camps où se trouvent les organisations humanitaires, bannies de certaines zones par le mouvement islamiste chabab.

Au Mali, l’armée signe une rare victoire après la prise de la ville stratégique de Kidal, désertée par les rebelles. Cette annonce de la reprise de cette ville devenue un bastion de la rébellion touareg intervient après une série de revers pour l’armée malienne.

Au Mali, la junte regagne du terrain en reprenant Kidal, fief des rebelles touareg. Les militaires maliens et leurs alliés russes avaient été chassés de la ville du Nord le 25 avril, durant l’offensive conjointe des indépendantistes du Front de libération de l’Azawad et des djihadistes du Groupe de soutien de l’islam et des musulmans.

Le journaliste nigérien Moussa Kaka est « en vie » et « détenu » par les autorités, selon Reporters sans frontières. Le sort du journaliste, directeur d’une télévision privée, suscitait de nombreuses inquiétudes depuis sa disparition, le 31 août.

« La France doit accorder l’asile au lanceur d’alerte et journaliste Ephrem Yalike-Ngonzo ». Dans une tribune au « Monde », Reporters sans frontières, le réseau Forbidden Stories et la Plateforme de protection des lanceurs d’alerte en Afrique exhortent les autorités françaises à octroyer l’asile au journaliste centrafricain, source exclusive d’une enquête sur la machine de propagande russe en Afrique.

Des troupes érythréennes sont entrées en Ethiopie, laissant craindre un affrontement direct avec Addis-Abeba. L’armée d’Asmara soutient les insurgés du Front populaire de libération du Tigré, en lutte contre le gouvernement central éthiopien. Des camions militaires et des équipements lourds érythréens ont été aperçus sur le territoire éthiopien.

En Egypte, les six journalistes du média d’investigation « Matsadaash » inculpés d’infractions liées au terrorisme. Les membres de la rédaction du site spécialisé dans le fact-checking avaient été arrêtés fin septembre lors d’un coup de force inédit contre des journalistes.

Finale de la CAN 2025 : le Tribunal arbitral du sport appelé à trancher entre le Maroc et le Sénégal. Pour avoir quitté la pelouse afin de dénoncer un penalty, les Sénégalais ont été déclarés forfaits malgré leur victoire face aux Marocains (1-0). Depuis, chacune des sélections revendique le titre continental : les premiers s’estiment vainqueurs sur le terrain, les seconds au nom du droit.

« Super El Niño » : frappé par une sécheresse historique, le Soudan du Sud s’apprête à affronter des inondations dévastatrices. Le ministère des ressources hydriques a alerté, mardi 6 octobre, sur la hausse des niveaux d’eau des bassins du lac Victoria et du Nil d’ici à décembre, qui pourraient atteindre leur maximum historique.

L’Union africaine lance sa propre agence de notation financière, pour « plus de justice ». L’agence, inaugurée mercredi 7 octobre à l’île Maurice, répond à une attente ancienne des milieux d’affaires africains, qui se considèrent comme défavorisés par les agences de notation occidentales. Ces dernières, en insistant sur les risques de défaut de paiement, les obligent à emprunter plus cher.

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi detained during protest against election chief. NEW DELHI: Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was detained by police Wednesday during a protest against the country’s election chief, as opposition parties intensified their campaign over a contentious revision of voter lists. Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were stopped by police as they marched toward Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in India’s capital New Delhi. Arab, GCC leaders condemn deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports. RIYADH: Arab and regional organizations strongly condemned Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports that killed three people and injured dozens, describing the strikes as violations of international law and threats to civilian safety. The attacks targeted Abha International Airport in Asir province, which borders Yemen, and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Syria seeks to revive cotton industry amid soaring costs and water scarcity. DAMASCUS: Across the agricultural heartlands of Syria, the hum of reopening cotton ginneries is offering a glimmer of hope to a cornerstonnee industry shattered by years of war, economic strain and neglect. Yet, from parched depressions in the west to irrigated riverbeds along the Euphrates, farmers and officials warn that soaring production costs, severe water shortages and the absence of clear pricing threaten to unravel the fragile recovery before it takes root. ‘A sun as black as my lungs’: how corruption crucified a polluted Albania city. The Albanian city of Elbasan was engulfed in smoke from its steelworks, revealing corruption and environmental mismanagement, with hazardous materials improperly stored at a local factory.

NASA Apollo pioneer Margaret Hamilton dies at 90. Margaret Hamilton, a pioneering computer scientist known for her work on NASA’s Apollo program, passed away at 90. She was instrumental in developing the software that helped land humans on the moon.

After botched US execution, Christa Pike was nearly taken off life support. Christa Pike, a convicted killer, regained consciousness after a failed execution and was nearly removed from life support. A court has ordered the preservation of evidence in her case.

El Nino will intensify, then peak in December: UN. The United Nations warns that El Nino will intensify and could become one of the strongest since 1950, impacting global temperatures and climate. This will peak in December, exacerbating climate change effects.

Tenzing Norgay’s son says Himalayas sending climate warning. Tenzing Norgay Sherpa’s son highlights how climate change is affecting the Himalayas and making mountaineering more dangerous. His comments come in conjunction with the release of the Apple TV film “Tenzing.”

UK Consulate in East Jerusalem to become mission after Israel orders closure. The UK Consulate General in East Jerusalem will remain operational, rebranded as a UK Mission, despite Israel's order to close it in response to British sanctions on Israeli settlements. While 20 diplomats will leave, a limited staff will continue to serve the Palestinian community, and Britain has ruled out taking reciprocal actions against Israel amid ongoing talks, despite escalating tensions between the two nations.

Pakistan military confirms deployment of forces to Saudi Arabia under Makkah pact. The Pakistani military has confirmed the deployment of troops to Saudi Arabia under the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, which was signed to ensure collective security following recent Houthi attacks. This trilateral pact, involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, underscores a long-standing military collaboration aimed at addressing regional threats.

US military told to prepare for resumption of large-scale operations against Iran – Axios. The Pentagon has instructed the US military’s Central Command to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale combat operations against Iran, though no specific launch date has been set. President Trump has not finalized the decision, but discussions suggest that extensive operations, potentially including bombings of key Iranian infrastructure, could occur before the upcoming US and Israeli elections.

On your bike! Bottas opts for two wheels to reach Singapore GP. Valtteri Bottas cycled 420 kilometers from Malaysia to Singapore for the Grand Prix, choosing a bike over a plane. This unique approach stands out among Formula One drivers.

PERTH: Oil prices rose on Thursday on persistent worries about supply from the key Middle East producing ‌region amid an increase in attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, while the US cut output as a hurricane menaced offshore production. Brent crude futures rose $2.28, or 2.28 percent, to $102.28 a barrel by 07:27 a.m. Saudi time. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained $1.66, or 1.88 percent, to $89.94. The Makkah Defense Alliance faces its first practical test. As the conflict with the Houthi militia escalates, the newly formed Makkah Defense Alliance, comprising Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye, convened an emergency meeting in Riyadh to establish its first formal command structure and operational protocols. The alliance, similar to NATO’s Article 5, emphasizes mutual military support in response to attacks, as tensions in Yemen intensify and external threats to Saudi security grow.

We seek a broader partnership with Saudi Arabia in advanced technologies – Taiwan’s top envoy. Taiwan's Foreign Minister Lin Chia-long expressed the nation's eagerness to enhance economic and investment ties with Saudi Arabia, particularly in advanced technologies like semiconductors and artificial intelligence, aligning with Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030. He emphasized Taiwan's role in the global semiconductor industry and highlighted the need for diversifying energy sources amid geopolitical tensions affecting supply routes.

Oscars: Saudi Arabia submits ‘A Matter of Life and Death’ for Best International Feature. DUBAI: The Saudi Film Commission has selected Anas Ba Tahaf’s “A Matter of Life and Death” as the Kingdom’s submission for the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards. Written by and starring Sarah Taibah, alongside Yaqoub Al-Farhan, the film is produced by Film Clinic, Front Row Filmed Entertainment and Arabia Pictures. Gulf chambers union discusses strengthening economic integration and market security. The 15th Consultative Meeting between the ministers of commerce and industry and the heads of federations and chambers of commerce and industry from the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states was held in Manama, Bahrain, where participants discussed the importance of strengthening ties between the government and private sectors across the GCC. Alcaraz feeling ‘mentally fresh’ ahead of Shanghai return. Carlos Alcaraz has expressed confidence and a refreshed mindset ahead of the Shanghai Masters following his recent success at the Japan Open. The world number three is still acclimating to the rigors of competitive play after recovering from a wrist injury.

Saudi Arabia, UAE set to drive GCC private credit growth: Moody’s. RIYADH: Saudi Arabia and the UAE are set to account for most of the Gulf’s private-credit growth as economic diversification and infrastructure spending create demand for financing beyond banks, Moody’s Ratings said. The Gulf Cooperation Council private-credit market is currently worth about $6 billion, compared with $1.8 trillion globally, but is expanding rapidly from a low base, the rating agency said in its latest report. Lebanese president says negotiations are alternative to war with Israel. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun stated that negotiations are a preferable alternative to war with Israel and emphasized that a formal agreement is necessary to resolve hostilities. He also expressed Lebanon's desire for any new force replacing UNIFIL to operate under UN auspices and highlighted the country's commitment to economic reforms and a strategic partnership with the EU.

I left Gaza, but my body is trapped in the horrors of war Submitted by Reem Salim on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 15:00 Ordinary sounds like the call to prayer, or the sight of an airplane overhead, still leave me tense and fearful Smoke and fire rise after an Israeli air strike on a house in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on 9 September 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP) On I left Gaza on 19 February 2024, but sometimes, it feels as though I am still trapped there. While I physically survived the war, its ghosts still haunt me through the memories spurred by certain sights and sounds, and in how my body involuntarily reacts. In Egypt today, the call to prayer, which is supposed to bring peace to my soul, leaves me tense and terrified. My heart races and I struggle to breathe, fearing that death is imminent. In October 2023, I was sitting with my family watching the news as the adhan from a nearby mosque minaret filled the air. Suddenly, I felt my body being thrown violently, as I choked on the smell of gunpowder. An intense Israeli bombardment had struck our neighbour’s house. A large piece of stone shattered the window a few centimetres from me. I gasped out the words of the shahada, believing I was about to die. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); To this day, every time the call to prayer reaches my ears, it takes me back to that moment. The war also triggered my fear of airplanes. When a plane flies over the skies of Egypt, I do not imagine an ordinary aircraft carrying passengers, but rather a fighter jet carrying missiles that could fall on us at any moment. Permanent damage These are not the only things that affect me. On one hand, I can still see the scars left by stitches around my middle finger, which looks different from the others; the nail no longer grows normally. It happened after we were displaced to my grandmother’s house in Deir al-Balah, amid repeated attacks on our own neighbourhood. Her house was crowded with other displaced people, and I was sitting in the dark one day when a missile exploded nearby. I feared that my younger brother, who could hear with only one ear, would lose his hearing in the other one from the force of the explosion - so I rushed towards him after hearing him cry, and told him to go to my mother. War on Gaza: Our memories of home will never die Read More » That was when another displaced child in the room, surely terrified by all that was happening around us, slammed the door in front of me, catching my finger between the door and its frame. The force severed the tip of my finger, tearing off my nail. At Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, my finger was stitched without anesthesia, as I cried from the severe pain. The wound healed, but the injury brought a new phobia: a fear of doors. Today, when I see someone place their hands near the side of a doorframe, my heart tightens and I grow tense. Beyond my memory and senses, the war took over part of my body, too. Sometimes, all it takes is for me to sit down to feel it. I was diagnosed with chronic inflammation in my tailbone as a result of sitting for long periods on a hard surface. The conditions of displacement forced me to sit on the floor all the time. I felt terrible pain, but hoped it was temporary and would disappear with time, planning to make an appointment with a specialist when the war ended. Instead, the pain became a permanent companion. One doctor in Egypt told me there was no option but to undergo surgery to remove the coccyx, which would itself have serious consequences - so I’ve learned to live with the pain. People say that time heals everything, but three years on, I have come to realise that the body has a memory that cannot be erased. It will continue to respond to certain sounds and scenes as though danger is still present. How can I say that I survived the war, when my body is still trapped in its horrors to this day? Submitted by Ana Maria Monjardino on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 14:36 Three founding members have quit the coalition since March, while South Africa faces accusations of 'hypocrisy' over coal shipments to Israel In this file photo, state representatives from South Africa and Colombia chair the opening conference of The Hague Group summit in Bogota, 15 July 2025 (Progressive International) Off Under former president Gustavo Petro, the Colombian state found it so difficult to halt coal shipments to Israel through diplomatic and bureaucratic channels that Petro called on the Wayuu , an Indigenous people of La Guajira, to occupy the train lines. Now, his right-wing successor has signed a decree resuming those exports, and Colombia has walked away from the Hague Group , the coalition it once co-chaired to hold Israel to account for breaches of international law. Its departure in August made it the third founding member, alongside Bolivia and Honduras, to leave the Hague Group in six months, leaving co-chair South Africa to steer the bloc alone. The Hague Group was founded in January 2025 by these nations, joined also by Cuba, Malaysia, Namibia and Senegal. "The Hague Group was born to advance international law in an era of impunity," South African Minister of International Relations Ronald Lamola told the meeting. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “Not only for the people of Gaza but for the future of a world where justice prevails over impunity,” the group agreed to take “coordinated legal and diplomatic measures” against Israel’s genocide in the midst of international failure to stop the carnage and complicity in Israel’s actions. This month, at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, 40 countries gathered to address how states can act collectively to ensure that international law is not merely proclaimed, but enforced. “It is also important to understand that The Hague Group is not a body that drafts, consolidates or passes new norms of international law,” explained Guillaume Long, diplomatic advisor to the Hague Group. Instead, it provides “a platform for states to try and articulate strategies, coordinate measures and have discussions,” he told Middle East Eye. However, he added, “the application of international law is usually at the domestic level.” The group is a kind of coalition of the willing attempting to ensure that international law is enforced in the face of a push by the United States and its allies to dismantle much of the global legal and humanitarian order. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella (L) and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (R) embrace during a bilateral agreement signing ceremony in Barranquilla, Colombia on 8 September 2026 (AFP) Political will is therefore essential. But in Latin America, a region where pink-wave politics once galvanised government support for Palestinians rights, the rise of a new right-wing order has led to the withdrawal of three founding Hague Group members. Meanwhile, as bombs continue falling on Gaza, ethnic cleansing escalates in the West Bank and the rule of law is under escalating threat from Palestine to Cuba, The Hague Group faces an up-hill battle. Losing Latin America In March, founding members Honduras and Bolivia promptly withdrew following the respective presidential victories of Nasry Asfura and Rodrigo Paz. Asfura, in particular, ramped up relations and extended a warm welcome to Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted for crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court (ICC), before even entering office. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Co-chair Colombia also withdrew in August, following the election as president of right-wing populist Abelardo de la Espriella. After less than two months in office, De La Espriella has appointed a new ambassador, recognised Israel's claim over the illegally occupied Golan Heights, abolished visa requirements for Israelis, restored the Colombia-Israel Free Trade Agreement, and withdrawn from South Africa's case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ). 'We are seeing Colombia deliver on what it offered: to boycott, sabotage, withdraw from multilateralism, and abandon its cause for Palestinian self-determination' - Guillaume Long, diplomatic adviser to The Hague Group But one of Petro’s former diplomats says the reversal is not simply a matter of presidential prerogative but may put Colombia in breach of its legal obligations. “The Colombian government has international obligations and is bound by international law,” said Mauricio Jaramillo Jassir, former deputy foreign minister of Colombia under Petro. “So while the constitution grants the president the authority and capacity to conduct diplomacy, that diplomacy must be managed within the framework of international law,” he told Middle East Eye, pointing to the binding legal obligation of third-party states to prevent and punish genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention. Colombia also withdrew the long-standing nomination of Colombian lawyer and former ambassador to the Netherlands, Carolina Olarte-Bacares, who co-led Colombia’s delegation in support of South Africa’s ICJ case against Israel, for an ICC judgeship. This leaves Latin America and the Caribbean without the possibility of representation despite representing 8.2 percent of the world’s population. “We are seeing Colombia deliver on what it offered: to boycott, sabotage, withdraw from multilateralism, and of course abandon its cause for Palestinian self-determination,” said Long. De La Espriella is following in the footsteps of US President Donald Trump who, alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is ramping up efforts to dismantle the ICC, in part an effort to buttress Israeli impunity. Doubling down during his UN General Assembly address this month, Trump called on members to resign from the “evil” and “rogue” institution. This onslaught against international institutions is not without opposition among the majority of UN member states, Long tells MEE, insisting that “there is a growing consensus that these attacks to destroy the institutions of international justice are completely outrageous”. 'Hypocrisy' at the ports At the BRICS summit in Delhi on 12 September, in a speech focused on inclusive global governance and strengthening the multinational system, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called for "comprehensive Security Council reform”. He pointed to the importance of accountability for atrocities, including “for the genocide committed against the people of Palestine”. Alongside accountability, implementation was central to the agenda of the meeting at the UN General Assembly this month. “The measures adopted in Bogota show that we are serious and that coordinated state action is possible,” announced Lamola at the summit, referring to an emergency meeting held in July 2025. Agreed upon by 13 states, those measures included a pledge to prevent the provision, transfer and transit of arms and dual-use items to Israel. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); And yet, in August 2025, after Petro issued a presidential decree banning coal exports to Israel, South Africa stepped in, allowing the Anglo-Swiss mining giant Glencore, which had supplied Colombian coal to Israel for decades, to relocate its core operations. It added that this is a “direct contradiction” to South Africa’s Hague Group commitments and as a result “South Africa is fuelling the ongoing genocide”. “The South African government talks ‘left’ by going to The Hague and walks ‘right’ by ignoring the sources of profit and trade,” said Patrick Bond, director of the Centre for Social Change at the University of Johannesburg. The export of coal bound for Israel from Richards Bay on South Africa's northeast coast “is the most extreme form of hypocrisy,” he explained. Bond previously told MEE that Ramaphosa’s government has every capacity to end coal exports to Israel through a category called dangerous exports. “The coal could be switched off immediately,” he said at the time. But the ruling elite of South Africa, including President Ramaphosa himself, has close ties to the extractive industry. In 2014, in order to assume the deputy presidency under Jacob Zuma, Ramaphosa was forced to divest his mining interests, including ownership of the Glencore-allied firm Shanduka, and his role as a local chairperson on the board of Optimum Coal, in which Glencore had a controlling interest. To this day, his brother-in-law, Patrice Motsepe, is the founder and non-executive chairman of African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) which operates ARM Coal in partnership with Glencore. As a result, ARM Coal holds access to Glencore’s “interest and entitlement” in Richards Bay. "It is because of the fact that states are not all in compliance with their third-state obligations that The Hague Group was created,” explained Long. “Our role in The Hague Group, regardless of what we may think or what we may personally consider to be the right course of action, is to try and consolidate coordinated state action,” he told MEE. The Hague Group is “a complex panorama of states that have done things with complex repercussions on the politics of their countries,” said Long. South Africa, for example, lost substantial US aid after launching its ICJ case against Israel. Likewise, Colombia’s Petro had his US visa revoked after calling for an armed front to directly oppose Israel’s genocide. How Gulf states are refinancing sovereign wealth funds as Iran war hits revenues Submitted by Ahmed Alqarout on Wed, 09/30/2026 - 17:27 A small group of US and Canadian firms now sit across Gulf energy infrastructure and money, as the boundaries between sovereign wealth and private capital are breaking down The logo for Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund is pictured during an event in Indian Wells, California, on 13 March 2024 (Matthew Stockman/Getty Images/AFP) Off Four Gulf states have rewritten the mandates of their main sovereign wealth funds since January. Officials have presented each change as long-planned institutional maturity. Not one has mentioned the Iran war , but wartime financial pressure signals the changes are being driven by fiscal recalculations as well. The restructuring accelerates a prewar trend. Since October 2023, Gulf funds have been cutting back spending and shifting towards narrower revenue-generating activities, as global geopolitical turmoil has driven up costs. In July, the state-owned Kuwait Oil Company put its crude pipeline network into a joint venture with US investment funds Blackstone and KKR, and Canada's Brookfield. The $16bn deal left the Kuwaiti side holding a 51 percent stake and leasing 13 pipelines back for 20.5 years, in exchange for a volume-based tariff. Kuwait took $7.85bn upfront. Kuwait spent the rest of the year building the law around deals like this, with new economic courts , an amended capital markets statute, and a plan to rewrite a quarter of its legislation by December. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); A few weeks ago, Kuwait issued a decree to let the treasury borrow from the Future Generations Fund, the pot set aside for the generation after oil. The 1976 law that created it had banned withdrawals outright. Borrowing is now capped at a tenth of the fund’s net assets, recorded as a debt owed back and repayable once the budget returns to surplus. Engine of growth Saudi Arabia , meanwhile, ran a deficit of 160 billion riyals ($42.6bn) in the first half of the year - its worst since 2016. The Public Investment Fund (PIF) was once filled by the state from oil receipts, but there is less to give now, so it raises its own funding. The PIF sold $2bn of sukuk , a type of financial certificate, in January, and a record $7bn of bonds in May , f or which investors bid around $29bn . The money ultimately goes into companies owned by the PIF, which return some of it as dividends and taxes to state coffers. The pressure is not expected to ease. The ministry's pre-budget statement for 2027 projects a deficit of 190 billion riyals ($50bn), around 3.6 percent of GDP, to be met by further borrowing and by what it calls alternative financing through project finance, infrastructure finance and export credit agencies. The PIF recently ordered spending cuts across more than 100 of its companies, slowing projects and laying people off, months before the board approved its 2026-30 plan this past April, splitting the fund into three portfolios named Vision, Strategic and Financial. The plan describes the fund moving from being the primary engine of growth to the steward of platforms that let others scale, while it facilitates borrowing and foreign investment. The funds are betting that the new borrowing will at least push the financial strain temporarily away, while new investment revenues come in before outstanding bills are due In September, PIF executives reportedly flew to New York with representatives from the AI firm Humain, the King Abdullah Financial District, and real-estate developer Red Sea Global, where they were set to meet investors from mega funds Apollo, Blackstone, Brookfield, Carlyle, KKR, Stonepeak and the US Export-Import Bank. The Saudis were reportedly looking for foreign backing amid cash constraints at home. Three of those firms had bought Kuwait’s pipelines two months earlier. For Qatar , companies at home are losing their earning power, and a fund that holds them is more expensive to borrow against. On 20 September, the prime minister carved roughly one-third out of the $580bn sovereign fund into a platform called Doha Investment , holding more than 40 companies, including Qatar Airways and Qatar National Bank. Its job is to back national champions, deepen capital markets and bring in international capital. It opened with a $60bn pipeline of opportunities, with $38.5bn in infrastructure projects, including public-private partnerships. Separated, each half carries its own risk profile. Lenders and investors now price Doha Investment on its own rather than against the whole fund, which lets Qatar borrow against its strongest assets on better terms and bring partners into the weaker ones. Boundaries dissolving Earlier in 2026, Abu Dhabi folded its wealth fund ADQ, worth $263bn, into a new vehicle called L’imad, with $300bn and more than 250 group subsidiary companies. In July, it brought in Boston Consulting Group and started calling itself an operationally active shareholder, rather than an investor. Last week, Bloomberg reported that L’imad was preparing to raise money from outside investors for a unit being built to back private equity funds and make its own deals. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The funds have not stopped their outside deals, but refocused them. Earlier in September, the US Federal Communications Commission cleared the way for 49.5 percent foreign ownership of Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros Discovery. Of that, three Gulf funds would hold 38.5 percent of non-voting equity: PIF with 15.1 percent, L’imad with 12.8 and the Qatar Investment Authority with 10.6. The deal has not closed, and litigation could push completion into 2027. Has US war on Iran killed the 'Gulf moment'? Read More » Days later, Qatar signed a memorandum with JPMorgan Asset Management for a $20bn partnership , $5bn of it lending to mid-sized American firms. JPMorgan then helped to arrange the Qatari state’s own $3bn bond issuance. A small group of American and Canadian firms now sit across Gulf energy infrastructure and Gulf money at the same time, lending against assets they will not operate while managing the cash those assets generate. The funds were built to hold what oil earned, and are now being run to earn what oil no longer does, while holding up budgets and state-owned companies. Slowly, the boundaries between sovereign wealth, fiscal financing and private capital are breaking down. The funds are betting that the new borrowing will at least push the financial strain temporarily away, while new investment revenues come in before outstanding bills are due. If so, the Gulf will have financed its transition with other people’s money, kept its savings, and come out with deeper capital markets and companies run to a standard outsiders are willing to pay for. Yet a struggling global economy may fail to deliver expected results. If revenues and borrowing do not pick up fast enough, these states will have less room to manoeuvre, and Gulf citizens will likely foot the bill in their livelihoods, which may increase social strains. Social spending cuts, higher taxes and an overall decline in quality of life would follow. Houthis warn staff to leave Saudi oil sites Yemen’s Houthi movement warned staff to leave Saudi oil facilities and claimed it had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile on Thursday. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital Riyadh.

Turkey assesses defensive support for Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement under a joint defence pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, with the countries agreeing on Monday to immediately implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan said Turkish and Pakistani military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defence, electronic warfare and technical support. “Yemen’s legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them,” Fidan said. He stressed that the agreement was defensive rather than offensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to conduct attacks from Saudi territory. “When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defence. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory,” Fidan said. Fidan said military delegations would assess Saudi Arabia’s operational defence requirements and determine what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could provide under the agreement. The comments come as Saudi Arabia faces continued attacks claimed by the Houthis, including missile launches towards Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition has said it intercepted ballistic missiles targeting the capital, while the Houthis have warned personnel to leave Saudi oil facilities and claimed responsibility for an attack on King Khalid International Airport.

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 8 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Capital police bar officers, personnel from using social media. ISLAMABAD: The capital police have banned the use of social media for all ranks, including officers and other employees, and have warned that strict departmental action will be taken in accordance with the relevant rules in case of any violation. In this regard, a policy was issued by the office of the police chief, Islamabad, bearing the signature of the deputy inspector general of police headquarters. According to the policy, all officers and officials, along with other staff, are directed not to speak at public forums in their official capacity, publish articles in print media, or express opinions or issue official statements on social media platforms without prior permission. Making videos or taking photographs while wearing a police uniform, whether in the premises of government buildings, vehicles or other private places for personal publicity or glorification is strictly prohibited. Furthermore, the policy restricts officers or officials from uploading, sharing, or disseminating any confidential or official document, photograph or their content on social media or any other media platform. Under this policy, the officers shall not share or express personal political or religious views on any media platform. Official channels for disseminating information regarding police activities shall be operated exclusively by the public relations branch, central police office. Unit heads shall be responsible for personally supervising and monitoring the activities of all officers and officials posted in their respective divisions, zones and units. In case of any violation, strict departmental action shall be taken in accordance with the relevant rules. The policy shall be implemented with immediate effect and shall remain in force until further orders. Officers, officials and personnel of all ranks shall ensure strict compliance with this policy. KP CM Afridi seeks law to impeach governor, rejects operations. • KP CM tells chief secretary, police chief not to follow ‘unconstitutional’ orders • Insists Centre’s counterterrorism approach failed; claims KP can restore peace within 100 days • Joins march supporters in Bara; says future strategy to be announced in Swabi • Kundi says governor’s rule, emergency will be imposed ‘to save KP’ PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday took strong exception to Governor Faisal Karim Kundi’s meeting with the chief secretary and provincial police chief and called for legislation to provide for the governor’s impeachment for “violating the Constitution”. “A prime minister and the chief minister can be sent home through a vote of no confidence. If there is no law, the KP Assembly will legislate [for impeachment of the governor] and nobody will be allowed to derail democracy,” Mr Afridi said. In a video message shared by his office, the chief minister accused the governor of acting unconstitutionally and attempting to provoke the provincial government but said his administration would continue to abide by the law and Constitution. “We will follow the Con­s­titution and that hurts ‘them’,” Mr Afridi said while chairing a meeting of the provincial cabinet. His remarks came a day after Governor Kundi cha­i­red a meeting with Chief Secretary Shahab Ali Shah and KP Police Chief Zulfiqar Hameed on the province’s security situation. Mr Afridi urged the two officials not to comply with any unconstitutional or illegal order from anyone. KP Advocate General Shah Faisal Utmankhel told the meeting that under Article 131 of the Constitution, the governor could seek information from the chief minister, but could not do so independently. “If I do not order you to take an unconstitutional step, do not obey if someone pushes you to follow any unconstitutional order,” Mr Afridi said. The chief minister direc­ted the chief secretary to advise the provincial admi­n­i­stration against involvement in any unconstitutional activity and ordered the inspector general of police to investigate firing on PTI workers in Upper South Waziristan. Mr Afridi accused the PPP-affiliated governor of staging a “drama” by convening the security meeting and termed the move unconstitutional. He said the provincial assembly, cabinet and government were fully functional and that such a meeting was unacceptable when the provincial government enjoyed a two-thirds majority. Turning his criticism towards the PPP, Mr Afridi blamed former president Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, along with Gen Yahya Khan, for the separation of East Pakistan and accused President Asif Ali Zardari of seeking to create a similar situation. “We will not allow any conspiracy to break up Pakistan to succeed,” he said, alleging that the PPP had always prioritised personal interests over national interests. Kundi raises governor’s rule Meanwhile, Governor Kundi said later on Wednesday that an emergency or governor’s rule would “definitely” be imposed in KP if the prime minister and the president considered it necessary to “save the province” amid the security situation. Speaking to Geo News , Mr Kundi said there had been precedents for the imposition of an emergency or governor’s rule. “In Balochistan, the PPP had to end its government for law and order and impose an emergency,” he said. Asked whether such a measure would be sustainable if imposed in KP, Mr Kundi said, “The first thing [to decide] is when and whether it is imposed. We can discuss its sustainability in another programme.” Counterterrorism policy Mr Afridi also reiterated his opposition to the Centre’s counterterrorism policy and said his government would not allow further military operations in the province. He maintained that terrorism had again been “imposed on the province” and said his government had worked to strengthen the police, Counter-Terrorism Depar­tment and Special Branch since he took office on Oct 15, 2025. Mr Afridi alleged that successive federal governments had imposed military operations on KP since 2004, displacing people who had still not received full compensation. He claimed nearly Rs100bn in compensation remained outstanding and said tribal families displaced from their homes had been promised Rs400,000 per household, but many had yet to receive the full amount. He also referred to a commitment to provide Rs370m to Rs380m a month to displaced people from North Waziristan living at the Baka Khel camp, stressing that the promised payments were still not being made. Mr Afridi said KP was fighting terrorism while also dealing with the consequences of federal policies and claimed peace could be restored within 100 days if the approach advocated by provincial stakeholders was adopted. He argued that the Centre’s counterterrorism policy had failed to bring peace either in KP or Balochistan and called for a change in approach. “A shift in policy is necessary. KP can establish peace within 100 days,” he said. Later on Wednesday, PTI workers from Bara, Jamrud and Landi Kotal welcomed the chief minister in his hometown of Bara as he travelled towards Peshawar as part of the party’s march. Addressing supporters from the top of a truck, Mr Afridi said no pressure tactic could weaken his resolve and again vowed not to allow further military operations in KP. He said the rights of the province would be pursued and announced that the future strategy for the march would be unveiled on reaching Swabi. The chief minister and participants in the march were expected to stay overnight in Bara before leaving for Peshawar on Thursday (today). Cabinet decisions The provincial cabinet approved forwarding to the federal government a joint resolution adopted by the KP Assembly condemning an incident in which the chief minister was allegedly taken away by Punjab Police in a vehicle, separated from his security detail and later left on the roadside without security during a visit to Punjab. The cabinet also approved obtaining $250m in World Bank financing for the READY-KP project under the bank’s applicable financing terms.
