Tiny French hamlet holds 'historic' cricket tournament. Visitors to the chateau in the tiny village of Liettres in northern France heard some unfamiliar terminology this weekend, at an international cricket tournament. “Howzat!” cried the players from France and Belgium taking part in the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478. The tournament, the brainchild of Lille Cricket Club, was launched in 2015 to celebrate the hamlet’s unlikely place in cricket history. According to organisers, Liettres was the site of the earliest recorded cricket match. Brussels’ player Sumit hits the ball during the international cricket match between Brussels and Arras as part of the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478, in Liettres on October 3, 2026.–AFP A letter written to King Louis XI in 1478 mentions an argument which broke out between a “poor gunner” at the Liettres castle called Estievenet Le Grant and a man called Cotaine Le Brasseur, who was playing “criquet” with others. Words led to blows, Le Brasseur was stabbed in the arm with a javelin, and later died from his wound. This reference pre-dates by around a century the first known mention of cricket in English sources, in court papers from 1589 mentioning that a pupil from Royal Grammar School in Guildford had been playing “creckett”. To celebrate the fact, the village contacted Philippe Dethoor, who was Lille president at the time, to ask if they would come down to put on a cricket workshop. The club had other ideas and decided to create a tournament. They secured access to a farmer’s field, rolled it and laid out a portable plastic wicket. Lille invited a team from Belgium, 12 Stars Brussels, and another one from Whitstable in Kent. “The English team were bowled out for 13 runs,” James Worstead, who was the Lille secretary at the time but now runs the leisure section at Viperes de Valenciennes, one of the invitees to the 2026 Liettres Challenge, told AFP. “Lille beat them for the loss of one wicket.” Brussels’ player Sumit hits the ball during the international cricket match between Brussels and Arras as part of the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478, in Liettres on October 3, 2026.–AFP Cricket connoisseurs Since then, the local authorities agreed to move the annual tournament to “a bumpy field behind the castle” and have also created a medieval fair around it including jugglers, fire-eaters, pony rides, axe throwing, a javelin tournament, Viking battles and, of course, a bouncy castle. “Initially, there were all these entertainment activities to attract people,” said Franck Pailleux, from the regional Bethune-Bruay tourism office. “But since the tournament was launched, we’ve noticed ever more interest in the game and people actually come to watch the matches – and they are connoisseurs.” Arras’ player Aslam prepares to hit the ball during the international cricket match between Brussels and Arras as part of the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478, in Liettres on October 3, 2026. .–AFP When the tournament was launched in 2015, it was widely covered in the British press, and even by one Indian media outlet. “Historians claim cricket was invented by the FRENCH,” screamed the Daily Mail in an article from August 30, 2015. But Dethoor insists that was not the case. “We never said that cricket was invented in France,” he said. “We know that cricket was codified in England. “As far as we know – and it wasn’t contradicted at the time – it’s the first written trace referring to a cricket match.” Worstead, who is an English teacher in nearby Valenciennes, said that there was “a good-humoured ambiguity” to the suggestion that cricket could have been invented in France. “There’s something quite iconoclastic about that,” he said. “Serious cricket historians do trace cricket back to Flanders and shepherds playing it. “So, it’s not quite as outrageous as it might seem. “But of course, for a tabloid headline, it’s: ‘The frogs say they’ve invented cricket’.” However, some experts in the field dispute the idea that the “criquet” in the letter to King Louis XI relates to the game. This photograph shows a view of the village’s castle, where the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478, an international cricket tournament, takes place in Liettres on October 3, 2026. –AFP Stretching the truth? Neil Robinson, head of heritage and collections at Marylebone Cricket Club, the guardians of the laws of the game, pointed to an article in the April 1973 issue of the Journal of the Society of Archivists. It includes a detailed analysis of the handwriting and concludes that the word “criquet” is in fact “etiquet” and refers to a stake being used in a game, which was probably not cricket. “I think it’s a pretty solid rebuttal and I think most historians who looked at it closely would probably agree with that,” said Robinson. Arras’ player bowls the ball during the international cricket match between Brussels and Arras as part of the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478, in Liettres on October 3, 2026. –AFP “It’s obviously a great story from the French point of view, but like so many other things in cricket history, I don’t think it happens to be true.” Still, there is a certain charm to the idea that a tiny hamlet of little more than 300 people could have a claim to a piece of cricket history. “I love to believe it because it gives them (the French) a certain belongingness to the game itself,” said Judson Daniel Raj Moses, the tour manager at 12 Stars Brussels, who this year lost to Lille in the final.

India denies bias in satellite internet approvals after Musk's 'oligarchs' jab. India defended its satellite internet approval process as fair and non-discriminatory on Thursday, hours after billionaire Elon Musk accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s ​launch in the South Asian nation. Starlink was being blocked by “certain oligarchs in order ‌to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people,” Musk wrote on X, without naming anyone. India’s telecom market is dominated by billionaires Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio and Sunil Mittal’s Bharti Airtel . Their ​satellite internet ventures, alongside Musk’s Starlink, have secured early approvals to launch in ​India but are awaiting spectrum assignment and final clearances. Airtel and Jio ⁠did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The wait has stretched on for four ​years for Starlink, following scrutiny over security requirements and access to spectrum. Responding to Musk’s comments, ​India’s telecommunications ministry said three entities were at broadly the same regulatory stage, with security assessments under way for each. It did not name the companies or Musk. “The suggestion that the framework or ​its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived,” the ministry said in ​a statement. The clash is not new. Musk has previously been at odds with Mittal and Ambani over ‌how India ⁠should grant them spectrum, before the three set aside their differences in 2025 to sign separate deals to distribute Starlink devices in India. India offers Starlink, part of Musk’s SpaceX, access to a satellite broadband market that Deloitte has forecast will be worth $1.9 billion by ​2030. The timing adds a ​diplomatic layer: the ⁠US has pushed Starlink’s market access as a goodwill marker in trade talks with tariff-hit countries , and New Delhi and Washington have struggled to finalise a trade deal since reaching a framework in ​February. Security concerns ⁠have also followed the recovery of Starlink equipment in India. Indian authorities have said they found Starlink devices in two separate operations in late 2024: a drug seizure by police in ⁠the ​Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army search in ​Manipur state. Musk then said Starlink’s satellite beams were “turned off over India” and were “never on in the first place”, ​a remark he repeated on Wednesday.

The growing protests against India's poll body — and PM Modi. India’s election commission is facing mounting pressure after a newspaper investigation alleged misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision. The Indian Express alleged last month that key decisions linked to the large-scale revision exercise — which has seen millions of names removed from draft voter rolls — were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners. The Election Commission of India (ECI), a constitutional body, has rejected the allegations. It says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid. Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters chant slogans, hold placards and wave national flag as they celebrate the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) examination paper leaks, following a protest, in Mumbai, India on July 26, 2026. —Reuters/File Opposition parties say legitimate voters are being struck off to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. Protests demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down have grown since the report, with a demonstration in the capital New Delhi on Saturday expected to draw large crowds. The allegations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi, in his third term in office, following student protests in July that forced the education minister to resign. Police detain a demonstrator during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India on October 3, 2026. — Reuters Here is a rundown of the major issues at stake in the latest protest: What’s the controversy? The Indian Express reported that the poll body has been riven by internal disagreements since the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter lists began in 2025. It said two of the ECI’s three commissioners formally lodged objections more than a dozen times in the last 10 months over key SIR decisions. Decisions by the three-member poll body should be taken by consensus or a majority. Why has it sparked anger? The poll body says the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from casting ballots. Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities. Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls. How many are excluded? According to election commission data cited by Indian media, more than 133 million names have been excluded from draft rolls. That’s roughly the population of Mexico and, in the world’s most populous nation, adds up to about 15 per cent of the electorate. Supporters of India’s main opposition Congress party try to remove a police barricade during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India on September 25, 2026. — Reuters The exclusions include duplicate entries and people found to have died. The final count of excluded voters, however, will only be clear after claims and objections are processed and final rolls are published. How big are the protests? Thousands have taken to the streets in protest, and the youth-led online Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement launched fresh demonstrations on October 2 in Mumbai. The opposition Congress Party has rallied in New Delhi, with key leader Rahul Gandhi briefly detained on both Tuesday and Wednesday. The CJP, which has millions of followers on social media, succeeded in its campaign to oust the education minister in July over irregularities in exam systems. The movement has called for another “mass mobilisation” on Saturday, supported by student groups aligned with left-wing parties. “Last time when we got together, it was a cabinet minister who had to resign,” said Neha Bora, a student leader who has emerged as one of the faces of the latest protests. “This time, we will see the CEC (chief election commissioner) being ousted.” Who is Kumar? Kumar, 62, is a retired civil servant from the elite Indian Administrative Service. He took charge as election commission chief in February last year and is due to remain in office until January 2029. supporter dressed as an electronic voting machine (EVM) holds a placard during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar organised by the Shiv Sena (UBT) and the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) in Mumbai, India, October 4, 2026. —Reuters Kumar’s civil services journey began in the southern state of Kerala, whose government launched a probe this month into corruption allegations involving him dating back to 2006. What do the courts say? The Supreme Court has ordered the government and election body to explain decisions linked to the voter-roll revision. The legality of the revision exercise has also been examined by the court. In May, it allowed the election commission to proceed with the nationwide exercise, while calling for safeguards to protect eligible voters. Another hearing is due next week.

Drones, explosions and soldiers in bulldozers: Surrounded by Israelis in Lebanon's 'model town'. Dodging the broken glass carpeting her home in southern Lebanon, Mariam al-Yaghi exited onto her upper balcony and pointed. A few hundred metres ​away was a sight the 67-year-old had grown accustomed to: military vehicles moving through the adjacent Lebanese village, still occupied by Israeli troops. Mariam al-Yaghi ,67, Lebanese resident from West Zawtar, stands in her damaged house in southern Lebanon, on October 1, 2026. — Reuters At night, Israeli soldiers patrol so close to Yaghi’s home in ‌West Zawtar that she can hear their voices. By day, she is often trailed by a small Israeli surveillance drone as she toils in her garden. Booms echo throughout the morning as Israel’s military destroys homes in the surrounding occupied towns with controlled detonations and bulldozers. “We hear them all the time from that house over there with the tile roof. We hear their voices yelling, the tanks when they move this way and that way. We hear all of that. They’re very close to us, but we’re sitting here and we’re not scared. Never,” Yaghi told ​ Reuters . Israeli troops withdrew from West Zawtar in July, the first test of a US-backed “pilot zone” plan for Israel to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon, in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah. Damaged homes in West Zawtar, southern Lebanon, on Oct 1, 2026. — Reuters But two months on, ​no further “pilot zones” have been agreed and residents of West Zawtar say their village is no blueprint. In response to questions from Reuters , the Israeli military said work to remove the ⁠threat of Hezbollah’s weapons had not been completed. Drones were used to identify threats, and restrictions on movement of local villagers were intended to protect troops. A US State Department spokesperson said the pilot zone process was “the only viable path” to ​security for both Lebanon and Israel. The zone would expand after the Lebanese army carried out clearance operations in the initial zone, and Hezbollah’s disarmament “is an integral part of this process”. Displaced resident of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, Zeinab Loubani, 54, reacts during an interview with Reuters at a school turned into a shelter for displaced families, in Sidon, Lebanon, on July 23, 2026. — Reuters Front-row seat to destruction Beginning seven months ago, more than a million ​Lebanese fled their homes when Israel launched air strikes and a ground invasion in parallel with the war in Iran , after the armed group Hezbollah fired into Israel in solidarity with Tehran. Ending the Lebanon conflict has been an Iranian condition for any peace deal, prompting Washington to press for an accord. But despite months of US-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel and a ceasefire agreed in June, Israel’s military has continued deadly strikes. Its troops still occupy a self-declared security zone that includes dozens of Lebanese villages, many of which the Israelis have demolished. Residents of West ​Zawtar say their return home in July was bittersweet: they were happy to be back, but found homes in ruins and Israeli troops uncomfortably close. A man walks next to damaged homes in West Zawtar, southern Lebanon, on Oct 1, 2026. — Reuters A tank shell had crashed into the upper floor of Yaghi’s home and all the windows had ​been blown out. Another had pierced her water tank’s roof, turning the water inside blood-red. Repairs will be costly, so Yaghi has delayed them for now. “We’ve put up cardboard and stuff like that because there’s no glass. My other son too, all the glass ‌and everything is ⁠gone. But here we are… until they get the hell out of here,” she said, gesturing towards the Israeli troops in the adjacent village. Few of Yaghi’s neighbours have returned so far, as their homes had been pulverised. Tank tracks ran through her garden, where olive trees she had nurtured for decades lay uprooted. With the harvest beginning, Yaghi was excited to pick whatever remained. Mariam al-Yaghi , 67, Lebanese resident from West Zawtar, stands in her damaged house in southern Lebanon, on Oct 1, 2026. — Reuters People whose groves lie near Israeli troop positions said they were requesting access to their trees through a US-led coordination mechanism between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries. Some mocked the absurdity of asking Washington for permission to pick olives. Others feared approval would come too late for the harvest. Just down the road from West Zawtar lies its twin village, East Zawtar, still occupied ​by Israeli troops who have been systematically demolishing it. ​ Displaced East Zawtar residents came to West Zawtar, where ⁠they sat on white plastic chairs in the main square with a front-row view of their home town across a small valley of olive groves and farmland. One man told Reuters he had seen lights on in his own house over the last three weeks, and expected Israeli troops were laying explosives to detonate it. “You try not to be upset, because it’s happened ​to so many people. But all it takes is one memory from the house, and you break down,” he said. Israeli troops gone, but keeping watch West Zawtar’s mayor, Abed ​Ezzedine, told Reuters the “pilot zone” programme ⁠had not worked, primarily because public services including electricity and running water were still largely unavailable. “In principle, I can tell you that no, it’s not successful. Based on what we were promised: that West Zawtar as a pilot zone would be a model town,” Ezzedine said. Mayor of Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh, Abed Ezzedin, stands in the outskirts of the village as he waits to return to his hometown, in southern Lebanon, on July 23, 2026. — Reuters Some 70 families had returned, mostly living in corners of their homes that had not been damaged. For many, it was a better option than paying rent elsewhere or living in a displacement shelter. The Lebanese state’s Council for the South has delivered ⁠16 prefabricated houses ​to families whose homes were uninhabitable. But most of the pre-fab dwellings are still unoccupied, with no access to electricity or water. State workers are ​beginning to extend electrical lines, but have had to run them further to a new station, as the village’s old connection ran through East Zawtar. “In a little bit, the drone might fly over people in the town square. It’s not leaving anyone alone,” Ezzedine said. Sure enough, a few moments later, a ​small surveillance drone flew over Ezzedine and a team of Reuters reporters, gradually dropping altitude until it was just a few meters overhead. It hovered for a few minutes, before flying towards the occupied neighbouring village. Header image: A man walks near rubble in West Zawtar, southern Lebanon, October 1, 2026. — Reuters

Nepra notifies consumers of Rs1.11 per unit higher fuel costs in Oct billing. ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) on Thursday notified electricity consumers of an additional burden of Rs16 billion by allowing Rs1.11 per unit in higher fuel costs in October billing. In a notification, Nepra said it had decided that the “positive fuel cost adjustment (FCA) for August 2026, i.e. Rs1.1086/kWh … shall be applicable to all the consumer categories of K-Electric and ex-Wapda distribution companies (XWDISCOs), except lifeline consumers, electric vehicle charging stations and prepaid electricity consumers of all categories who opted for the prepaid tariff”. The regulator said the higher FCA would also be applicable to consumers under the incremental consumption package. DISCOs and KE are required to reflect the fuel cost adjustment for August 2026 in the October 2026 billing month. The Central Power Purchasing Agency (CPPA) had reported that the actual average fuel charges component for August 2026 amounted to Rs8.8265/kWh, against the reference fuel charges component of Rs7.0998/kWh approved in the applicable notified consumer-end tariff. Accordingly, it had demanded an additional FCA of Rs1.73 per unit for electricity consumed in August 2026. After certain adjustments, Nepra worked out the actual fuel component of the tariff at Rs8.2084, instead of Rs8.8265 as claimed by CPPA, thus allowing an additional FCA of Rs1.11 in October billing, instead of the Rs1.73 per unit demanded by CPPA. The higher additional fuel cost in August stemmed from expensive RLNG imports from the spot market, as contracted supplies from Qatar remained under force majeure, besides higher coal imports and lower-than-estimated availability of cheaper hydropower and nuclear generation. Hydropower was originally targeted to account for about 41 per cent of total power generation, but its share was slightly below 38pc, while the share of nuclear power was estimated at 16.4pc but turned out to be 10pc due to an outage at the Karachi’s nuclear power plants. As a consequence, the share of imported coal-based generation increased to 15.6pc, instead of 7.4pc as originally planned. Hydropower has no fuel cost, while the average nuclear fuel cost increased to Rs3.15 per unit due to lower utilisation, instead of Rs2.5 per unit. In contrast, the cost of imported coal-based generation came to Rs17 per unit. The cost of local coal-based generation was reported at Rs5.5 per unit. The cost of RLNG-based generation was reported at Rs45.93 per unit, even higher than the Rs45.25 per unit cost of furnace oil-based power generation, which also includes a petroleum levy of Rs73,000 per tonne. The FCA is reviewed every month under the tariff regime applicable across the country and is usually applicable to consumers’ bills for one month only. Under the tariff mechanism, changes in fuel costs are passed on to consumers only on a monthly basis through an automatic mechanism, while quarterly tariff adjustments on account of variations in power purchase prices, capacity charges, variable operation and maintenance costs, and use-of-system charges — including the impact of transmission and distribution losses — are built into the base tariff by the federal government.

Canadian writer Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the award-giving body said on Thursday. The prize is awarded by the Swedish Academy and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m). Canadian poet and essayist Carson’s work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix. She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work which ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as Autobiography of Red from 1998. Her style is exemplified in Norma Jeane Baker of Troy from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play Helen and Marilyn Monroe. Carson takes a place beside luminaries such as Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Alice Munro and Ernest Hemingway as a recipient of the award, which often divides opinion among book lovers. The Academy has been lambasted for ignoring some of the literary titans of the last 120 years such as Leo Tolstoy, Virginia Woolf and Jorge Luis Borges, criticised for snubbing US authors, though it gave the prize to singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in 2016, and accused of being too obscure in its choices. Defenders say the Academy has made popular picks, such as Colombia’s Gabriel Garcia Marquez in 1982 and Doris Lessing in 2007, arguing that part of its task is to highlight lesser-known literary traditions and encourage readers to broaden their horizons. Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901. Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai , dubbed the “master of the apocalypse” by American critic Susan Sontag.

Turkiye's FM Fidan says Istanbul assessing aid to Saudi Arabia as part of Makkah agreement. Turkiye is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia counter attacks from Yemen’s Houthis under the Makkah defence pact signed between Islamabad, Riyadh and Istanbul, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday. The defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. “The technical evaluations are [being] carried out, and these continue among our military officials,” Fidan said during a joint press conference in Ankara with his Hungarian counterpart, adding that officials were working out what contributions could be made, particularly on air defence. Ankara’s top diplomat also stressed that the pact was a defensive agreement, not an offensive one. “When a country of this agreement is attacked, you have to side with them,” Fidan stated. “This is not an attack agreement. Turkiye is not carrying out an attack by sending troops to another country’s land.” The Turkish foreign minister added that the process of sending the text of the agreement to the Turkish parliament for ratification had been finalised. Fidan’s remarks came after Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Monday agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Riyadh. The emergency meeting of the alliance’s Strategic Political and Defence Committee addressed the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia. “The committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats,” a statement issued by the Foreign Office after the meeting said. While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development comes against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in the Yemen conflict. A day prior, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told CNN that Pakistani troops were already in Saudi Arabia, adding that they had been in the kingdom “for decades” and across multiple domains. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has also described the agreement as defensive, without an offensive agenda. Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has said Pakistani and Turkish forces would play a supporting role, including reconnaissance, while Saudi forces conduct combat operations.

Mobile services reportedly non-functional in parts of Peshawar ahead of PTI march’s expected arrival. PESHAWAR: Large parts of the provincial capital reportedly remained without mobile and cellular internet services on Thursday in an unannounced suspension that started last night, Dawn has learnt. The move comes as PTI’s long march, launched on Oct 4 from Lakki Marwat, is set to reach Peshawar today according to PTI’s schedule. The protest march to demand the release of party founder and ex-premier Imran Khan had reached the Khyber district by Wednesday evening. Though there was no word from the provincial government on the unannounced cellular disruption, a Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) official, however, confirmed to Dawn that the authority had ordered the suspension at the directives of higher authorities. The official told Dawn the suspension was temporary and taken as a security precaution during the long march. The official said the ministry orders were conveyed on Wednesday night. Special Assistant to the Chief Minister on Home and Tribal Affairs Tariq Saeed Marwat did not respond to whether his department requested the interior ministry cell phone service suspension. KP Information Minister Shafi Jan was also not available for comment. Meanwhile, some major private schools across Peshawar also remained closed on Thursday. However, government schools, colleges and universities remained open. Many parents found out about the school closure on Thursday morning when their children returned home after finding the school gates locked. Yousaf Khan, a resident of Ring Road, told Dawn that he found out on Thursday morning. “My children were told at the school gate to go back,” he said, adding that he did not hear about the closure due to the suspension of cellular service. “Due to the prevailing political situation in the city, the school will remain closed tomorrow, i.e, on Oct 8”, a notice from one of the private schools read, adding that classes will resume from Friday. However, Private Schools Regulatory Authority (PSRA) officials said no order for school closure was issued, and action will be taken against schools that remained closed without government directions. The authority has also written to the principals of all private schools, stating that certain private educational institutions had been closed by their respective administrations in connection with the ongoing long march, without any notification from the PSRA. “In view of the above, all heads/principals/administrators of private educational institutions are hereby directed to keep their respective institutions open and ensure regular academic activities until clear directions/notification are issued by this authority,” the letter, seen by Dawn , read. It said that failure to comply with the directions would be viewed seriously, and strict disciplinary action would be initiated against the concerned institution/management under the relevant rules and regulations. PTI’s march began from Lakki Marwat on Oct 4, from where the protesters trekked to Kohat on the second day and arrived in Mattani, located on the outskirts of Peshawar, that night. While the plan for the trek after Oct 8 is yet to be announced, the PTI previously announced Islamabad as its final destination. The Centre has warned the party against any protests or gatherings in Islamabad. However, the PTI decided to embark on the march after weekend talks with the federal government failed to bridge their differences for multiple reasons , particularly over the counterterrorism policy. Gohar calls for reviewing counterterrorism policy PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan said on Thursday that his party had never supported terrorism, adding that, however, the country’s counterterrorism policy needed to be reviewed in the light of changing circumstances. Gohar was speaking to the media in Charsadda, which is expected to be the next stop of the PTI’s march after Peshawar. The PTI chairperson visited the residences of KP Public Health Engineering Minister Fazal Shakoor and MNA Fazal Mohammad Khan, whom the PTI alleges were abducted by unidentified men amid reports of detentions of its workers and members ahead of the march. Gohar expressed concern over their disappearance and demanded their immediate and safe recovery. Speaking to the media at their residences, he noted that 18 days had passed since Shakoor’s alleged abduction and his family had no information about his whereabouts. He urged the relevant authorities to take immediate notice of the matter and ensure that Shakoor and Khan were recovered and reunited with their families. PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan speaks to the media in Charsadda on Oct 8. — Photo by Faiz Muhammad Gohar said the “enforced disappearances” were a matter of serious concern and stressed the need for rule of law and protection of citizens’ constitutional rights. If such incidents were taking place in KP, they could also occur in other provinces, he further warned. He also rejected the imposition of governor’s rule or an emergency as a solution to the prevailing situation in KP, as federal ministers continue to indicate the possible enforcement of either of the two, citing terrorism. The warning of a possible emergency or governor’s rule had come ahead of the PTI’s long and as talks between the opposition party in the Centre and the federal government failed earlier this month. For his part, Gohar said political issues should be resolved through constitutional and democratic means. He called upon the decision-makers to respect the public mandate and elected governments. On the security situation, he asserted that the PTI, its workers and supporters had never supported terrorism. He said the party stood with the state in the fight against terrorism, but the country’s policy on the issue needed to be reviewed in light of changing circumstances. “Terrorism, whether in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan or Sindh, is against Pakistan,” he said, adding that the loss of any Pakistani’s life in the fight against terrorism was a national loss. He called for the implementation of the National Action Plan through a unified national policy rather than politicising the issue. Gohar also defended CM Afridi, saying he had never issued a statement in support of terrorists. He criticised what he described as attempts by some federal ministers to portray PTI as a supporter of terrorism. The PTI chairperson said his party was still ready for meaningful and positive dialogue with its political opponents and expressed hope that Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman would play a constructive role in the prevailing situation. He thanked the JUI-F, Awami National Party and Jamaat-i-Islami for opposing the imposition of governor’s rule. On the PTI’s long march, he said it would continue as per the decided schedule, with gatherings planned in Mardan on Oct 10 and Swabi on Oct 11, after which the future course of action would be decided by the party leadership. He also criticised the imposition of Section 144 in parts of KP, saying elected representatives should be taken into confidence in matters concerning law and order. He urged all political parties, whether in government or opposition, to play their role in strengthening democracy, an independent judiciary, free elections and the rule of law. Gohar said the federal government and the opposition needed to set aside their differences and engage in sincere, unconditional dialogue to help the country overcome its political crisis. PHC seeks CM Afridi’s reply to contempt plea Separately, the Peshawar High Court (PHC) on Thursday sought a reply from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi to a contempt petition alleging that he violated a court order by using an official helicopter to participate in the PTI long march. A bench comprising Chief Justice SM Attique Shah and Justice Ijaz Khan issued notice to the chief minister on a petition filed by PML-N MPA Zahir Khan. The petitioner alleged that the chief minister violated the court’s Oct 23, 2025 judgment , which barred the use of government vehicles, machinery and manpower for protests, rallies, long marches or political activities. According to the petition, Afridi used a KP government helicopter on Oct 4 to travel from Peshawar to Lakki Marwat to participate in, launch and lead the PTI’s long march. He contended that the violation was not confined merely to the CM’s journey, but the official helicopter’s use necessarily involved deployment of its pilots, crew, fuel, technical staff, ground arrangements, security personnel, protocol officials and other public resources. He added that the entire official machinery accompanying and facilitating the said flight was employed to enable the chief minister to reach and lead the political long march, in direct violation of the 2025 ruling. The petitioner sought contempt proceedings against CM Afridi and asked the court to summon him and seek details of the helicopter’s authorisation, flight log and expenditure. The hearing was then adjourned.

Pakistan Bar Council declares Ahsan Bhoon's law degrees genuine. ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) on Thursday declared that the degrees of its elected members, including prominent lawyer Ahsan Bhoon, were genuine. The announcement by the PBC — the supreme regulatory body of lawyers — follows a debate over lawyers’ degrees, with the qualification of Bhoon, a member of the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP), particularly being questioned . In an official statement on Thursday, the PBC noted that the returning officers (ROs) for the council’s 2020 and 2025 elections had gotten the elected members’ degrees verified from their respective universities before notifying them as PBC members. “It is, therefore, clarified that the verification of the degrees of the returned candidates, including that of Bhoon, was undertaken through the relevant universities in accordance with the prescribed procedure,” the council said. It explained that the RO for PBC Election-2020 , the Attorney General for Pakistan (AGP), had the degrees verified by the universities soon after the elections, following which the successful candidates were notified as PBC members. Similarly, the RO for PBC Election-2025 , also the AGP, again initiated the process of verification of the elected members’ degrees. “Some members whose degrees were already verified in the last elections, their degrees too were sent again for verification to the relevant universities as well as the Higher Education Commission (HEC),” the council maintained. The statement comes over a week after former MNA and retired Capt Muhammad Safdar called for verification of the degrees of prominent lawyers, including Bhoon, a close associate of Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar. The debate also comes ahead of the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) elections scheduled for Oct 29. Bhoon, a former SCBA president, heads the Independent Group, also known as the Asma Jahangir Group. Safdar has announced the formation of his own group, the Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah Group. Days later, Safdar moved a complaint with the JCP to seek verification of Bhoon’s educational qualifications, enrolment and professional credentials. The complaint had also sought verification of his original degrees, transcripts, result cards and registration records; independent confirmation from the degree-awarding institution; verification from the HEC; his complete enrolment record with the relevant provincial bar council and the PBC; and the dates and basis of his enrolment as an advocate. On the other hand, Bhoon has served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Capt Safdar, demanding an unconditional public apology and retraction of the allegation that his LLB degree was fake. According to the notice, Safdar made the allegations while speaking publicly outside the Supreme Court on or about Sept 23, with remarks repeated in later media appearances and video messages.

French teens march for decent schools despite government's pledge to act. French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday as the government promised to address their grievances about teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings but gave few specific details. The protest movement, now into its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under pressure from bond markets to reduce its debt and deficit. High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students at a large march in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions. She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class. Protesters face French CRS riot police outside Lycee Helene-Boucher high school as students block the road, during nationwide protests in Paris, France, October 8, 2026, to demand better school conditions. —Reuters “At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study,” she said. Di Sciullo, 28, was carrying a placard that read “I’m a teacher and my students help me catch cockroaches in class.” Protesters march during a demonstration by French high school students in Marseille, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades, expressing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment, in Marseille, France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Minister promises urgent action Education ministry figures showed the number of school blockades was gradually decreasing. It said 224 were closed in the morning, down to 157 by lunchtime, meaning that 96 per cent of schools were open. Scuffles between police and protesters took place at some blockade locations in Paris. Large crowds demonstrated across the country from Lille in the north to Rennes and Nantes in the west, the capital Paris, and Toulon and Marseille in the south. Police officers stand guard as French high school students block the road outside Lycee Helene-Boucher high school, as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in Paris, France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Education Minister Edouard Geffray held a meeting with students and teachers at a high school in the eastern city of Reims. “I am currently implementing an emergency plan to ensure that absent teachers can be replaced on a long-term basis,” he said afterwards, adding that heavy school timetables were also under review. It is not uncommon for French teenagers to have lessons from 8am to 6pm, as well as large amounts of homework. French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Nantes as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions in France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Hundreds of arrests Geffray also said he was working on potential improvements to Parcoursup, the national online portal for applying to university, which has been widely criticised as confusing and stressful for applicants. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged late on Wednesday that the government would present “concrete, quick and fully funded responses” to the protests by late October, without offering specifics. French students gather outside the Lycee Henri-IV in Paris as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters A prominent complaint featured on banners and placards was that the police response to the wave of protests has been too heavy-handed. “Too young to be listened to, old enough to be tear-gassed” was one example. There have been hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries since the movement started. On Wednesday, the government suspended the use of stun grenades in the policing of the protests after one teenager’s hand was blown off. Polarised political response as election looms Six months out from an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron after the end of his second consecutive term, politicians’ responses to the wave of student protests have been starkly polarised. Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen has highlighted damage to schools caused by a minority of protesters and called for them or their parents to foot repair bills. On Tuesday, she outlined plans to slash public spending should she win. rotesters clash with French gendarmes, as French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Nantes as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions in France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon, who also has a chance of making the runoff, has praised the protesters as “incredible” and denounced police brutality. According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV , 72pc of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate, but 55pc of them think the protests should stop. The government has sought to tread a line between condemning violent incidents in which schools were set ablaze and staff injured, while also expressing sympathy with some of the students’ complaints. Students protest in Belgium too On Thursday, student protests were also taking place in the Belgian cities of Brussels, Ciney and Liege. Grievances included rising costs, overcrowded classrooms, limited resources and increased teacher workloads. In Liege, where police said almost 200 arrests had been made in connection with student protests this month, authorities have imposed a ban on public gatherings of more than three people until October 16. However, police said a gathering in front of the city’s university had been authorised.

Israel drastically reduces British diplomatic presence in Jerusalem, announces closure of consulate. Israel said the British consulate in Jerusalem ended its functions on Thursday but that seven diplomats would be allowed to remain in a limited capacity, with the United Kingdom saying it would continue to offer “vital services”. The move comes after Israel ordered the closure of the consulate in September as retaliation after London led Western sanctions over violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Thursday’s move to downsize the UK presence had followed a dialogue with the British government in order to avoid an escalation of tensions between the two countries. “As I announced, the British consulate in Jerusalem ended its role today,” Saar said in a statement, adding that 20 diplomats including the consul general were ending their missions and leaving the country. Saar said the building is the property of the British government and that a “task force of only seven diplomats” would be allowed to operate from the premises, “which ceased to function as a consulate today”. “Their scope of activity will be very limited,” Saar said. Britain and Israel have “agreed on the continuation of dialogue between the governments, within which both sides will be able to raise issues important to them”, he said. The UK government pledged to continue delivering “vital services” in Jerusalem, saying the consulate general building would remain open and would “be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem”. “The UK Mission, Jerusalem is independent, operational and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people,” British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said in a statement. Miliband said the UK did not accept that the Israeli government had “the legal right” to enforce the closure. “We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible,” he added. Israeli settlements An AFP photographer on Thursday saw that the diplomatic emblem and a plaque that adorned the consulate’s facade had been removed. The measure has led Britain to lose a “historic and meaningful presence” in terms of their support for the Palestinians and having a consulate general in Jerusalem, an Israeli diplomatic source said. “So yes, they keep the building” and a limited number of diplomats, the source told AFP , but “they have lost a historic and significant footprint”. The source said they thought the recent dialogue between the British and Israeli governments would allow a “turning point” in deteriorating relations. “If until a few weeks ago, until Sept 8, we were on a path of spiralling down, then I think the page has turned, and we are now on a path that will enable a return to more constructive, not only dialogue,” the source said. “Dialogue is a path towards returning to … more constructive relations,” they added. On Sept 8, Saar ordered the British consulate to close. He said Israel would also expel British representatives at a centre monitoring the US-brokered ceasefire plan in Gaza , bar British training for Palestinian Authority forces and ban 12 Britons, mostly members of parliament, from visiting. Saar on Thursday said the measures had been implemented. The retaliation came after 12 countries including Britain, Canada and France announced they would sanction trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, following a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians in the occupied territory. The British consulate in Jerusalem was founded nearly 200 years ago. It lies in east Jerusalem, part of the historically Palestinian area that Israel captured in 1967. Israel later annexed east Jerusalem and considers the holy city its undivided capital. While Israel controls east Jerusalem, most countries including Britain do not recognise its sovereignty over the whole city. The British consulate handles “political, commercial, security and economic interests between the UK and Palestine”, according to its website as well as providing consular services to British nationals in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza.

Pakistan waging ‘global war’ against terrorism, Naqvi tells UN chief on last day of his visit. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Thursday said Pakistan was waging a global war against terrorism as he met with United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres. The two, along with Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, discussed global and regional issues and matters relating to peacekeeping missions. Naqvi told the UN chief that 25 terrorist organisations were operating in Afghanistan, posing a threat to global peace. “The international community needs to work together to tackle this threat,” he said. Naqvi reaffirmed that Pakistan would continue to play its role in UN peacekeeping missions, adding that Pakistani personnel were also serving in the UN police. He added that 181 Pakistanis had sacrificed their lives in peacekeeping missions. The UN chief recognised Pakistan’s participation in peacekeeping missions, saying it had always been “prominent”. “Pakistan’s role in world peace is commendable,” Guterres said. After the meeting, Guterres concluded his two-day visit to Pakistan, which “provided an important opportunity to reaffirm Pakistan’s longstanding partnership with the United Nations”, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement. The UN chief’s visit highlighted “Pakistan’s unwavering support for multilateralism”, FO said. Previously, Guterres also met President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar. On Tuesday , in a meeting with Guterres, Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to the UN charter, multilateralism and settlement of disputes through dialogue and diplomacy. Dar “also highlighted Pakistan’s ongoing diplomatic efforts in support of regional peace and stability”, FO said. While briefing the UN chief on India’s violation of the Indus Water Treaty and international law, Dar “reiterated Pakistan’s call for a just and peaceful resolution of the Jammu & Kashmir dispute”. He further highlighted Pakistan’s support for Palestinians and their “legitimate struggle for self-determination and statehood”, FO said. “The two sides also exchanged views on regional and international peace and security, including Afghanistan and counter-terrorism, as well as sustainable development, climate change, and the future of multilateralism.” President Zardari on Tuesday conferred Nishan-i-Imtiaz on the UN chief “in recognition of his distinguished international service and contribution to global peace and development”. On Wednesday , Guterres “exchanged views on issues of regional and international importance” in meeting with PM Shehbaz, according to FO. Guterres “commended Pakistan’s longstanding contribution to the United Nations, including its significant role in UN peacekeeping and its efforts to promote dialogue, mediation, and international cooperation”, FO said. The UN chief was also briefed on Pakistan’s progress in disaster preparedness and early warning systems by the National Disaster Management Authority. On Wednesday, Guterres, in his address during a special talk at the Foreign Service Academy, “reflected on his longstanding association with Pakistan and highlighted the generosity, resilience, and solidarity of the Pakistani people”. Guterres’ first visit to Pakistan as the UN secretary general was in February 2020, about three years after he was elected to the position in 2016. His 10-year tenure as UN chief is set to end on Dec 31.

Bahrain working to 'speed up' approval of Pak-GCC free trade pact, foreign minister says. Bahrain on Thursday said it was working to “speed up” the approval of a free trade agreement between Pakistan and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The remarks came after the two countries held the third session of their Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC) in Islamabad. Bahrain’s FM Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani — who arrived in Pakistan last night on a two-day visit — co-chaired the JMC session along with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. Addressing a joint press briefing with Dar, the Bahraini minister noted that the JMC meeting covered “more than 15 fields”. He said both sides agreed to establish a joint working group on trade and investment, as well as to convene the joint working group on energy next month on oil, gas and minerals. They also agreed to take forward cooperation in food security, information technology, law enforcement, media, labour mobility, health, education, culture and sports. “We also committed to finalising the GCC-Pakistan free trade agreement,” he said, referring to the potential deal that was said to be near finalisation in late 2025. The minister said that Bahrain, having the GCC presidency, was working to “speed up the signing or the approval of the GCC-Pakistan FTA”. Responding to a query, the visiting dignitary described the bilateral relationship between Pakistan and Bahrain as “very healthy and strong”. He added that it was “radiant and well-looked after” by Bahrain’s King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and Crown Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa. “It is really valued by the people of Bahrain,” he added. Highlighting recent bilateral exchanges between their countries, FM Al Zayani said: “We have a very truthful relationship; we are so frank with each other. We understand the constraints on each other and work accordingly.” Emphasising the consistency in their ties, with no “ups and downs”, he said, “We are consistent and growing. We feel safe in this relationship.” Al Zayani expressed Manama’s appreciation for Islamabad’s “principled positions on the ongoing crisis”, including its support in March for a United Nations Security Council resolution condemning Iranian attacks on GCC countries. The minister also praised Pakistan’s “efforts alongside other partners to facilitate US-Iran dialogue and de-escalation, including by hosting the Islamabad Talks ” in April. The Bahrain FM went on to strongly condemn the recent deadly “terrorist attacks” on Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport. He also condemned the “Houthi terrorist militia’s attacks on civilians and civilian facilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its assault” on the holy cities of Makkah and Madina . Noting that targeting of civilian facilities was a “flagrant violation” of international law, Al Zayani affirmed Bahrain’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia “whose security is an integral part of our own and of the GCC”. The Bahrain FM said he and Dar also discussed the crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, where “commercial vessels continue to come under attack”. They underscored the importance of freedom and safety of navigation and respect for international law, he added. Al Zayani vowed Bahrain and Pakistan will continue “close coordination” at the UNSC and between their Missions in New York. Furthermore, the visiting FM noted that the two countries will mark 55 years of diplomatic relations on Oct 14. Al Zayani remarked that the “bonds of brotherhood, trust and solidarity […] gained fresh momentum with the official visits to Bahrain” of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in November 2025 and of President Asif Ali Zardari in January this year. The minister noted that more than 140,000 Pakistanis in Bahrain contributed to its progress and “form a living bridge between our peoples”. The Bahrain FM said he would also meet with PM Shehbaz, President Zardari and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir during his visit. Gulf situation, Palestine, IWT discussed In his remarks, Dar thanked Al Zayani and his delegation for “their constructive engagement and their very valuable contribution to the success of today’s JMC session”. Noting that the discussions were held in a cordial and constructive atmosphere, he said both sides “reaffirmed our shared commitment to further strengthening bilateral cooperation across a broad spectrum of sectors”. “A key outcome of the session was the strengthening of our institutional framework through the operationalisation of several joint working groups,” Dar said, adding that these mechanisms will help ensure effective implementation of the decisions taken by the JMC. “Both sides also agreed to enhance cooperation in trade and investment promotion, industrial collaboration, agriculture and food security, skills development, higher education, information technology, logistics and maritime affairs, among many other areas.” They “particularly welcomed closer engagement between the business communities of the two countries”, the deputy premier added. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in labour mobility, vocational training and human resource development, with a view to creating new opportunities for skilled Pakistani professionals and workers. Dar noted that he and Al Zayani also exchanged views on the “evolving situation in the Gulf and emphasised the importance of restraint, de-escalation, dialogue and diplomacy”. “We discussed the need to ensure the safety and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab, given their importance to regional and global food and energy security.” The ministers also discussed the “grave situation in Palestine” and expressed concern over the “continued expansion of illegal settlements and attempts to alter the status of Al-Quds Al-Sharif”. Dar also raised the issue of India’s unilateral decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, terming it a “material breach of international law”. “Such actions jeopardise the water, food and energy security of Pakistan’s 250 million people,” the deputy premier stressed. “Pakistan-Bahrain friendship remains strong and forward-looking, and we are brotherly nations, with long fraternal ties, cooperating on international foras and meeting very frequently wherever we get an opportunity like brothers,” the DPM affirmed. He expressed Pakistan’s commitment to “building an even more prosperous future together, God-willing, and taking the trade and economic ties to a new height”. Dar said Islamabad looked forward to the convening of the JMC’s fourth session in Bahrain in 2027, as both sides will try to hold the meetings every year. President Zardari meets Bahrain FM Separately, President Zardari met with the Bahrain foreign minister, who called on him at the President House. According to a press release by the president’s secretariat, the two leaders first held a restricted meeting, which was followed by a delegation-level meeting. Zardari, in conversation with Al Zayani, said that Pakistan was “keen to translate strong bilateral political relations into deeper trade and investment ties”, according to the statement. Noting that the country attached “great importance” to its relations with Bahrain, he expressed the desire to further strengthen bilateral cooperation, highlighting opportunities for this cooperation in “food security, IT and digital services, construction, mining, port handling, research and development, tourism and healthcare”. He also encouraged greater business-to-business engagement between the two countries. “The president appreciated Bahrain’s warm welcome of the Islamabad MoU and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and its recognition of Pakistan’s efforts for regional peace, security and stability,” the press release said. It added that President Zardari also appreciated Bahrain’s support and opportunities for over 134,000 Pakistanis residing in the kingdom, and welcomed continued cooperation on matters regarding the Pakistani diaspora. “The president said Pakistan and Bahrain share a long-standing and trusted defence partnership, reflected in joint exercises, high-level exchanges and institutional cooperation,” it said, adding that he expressed Pakistan’s readiness to further strengthen cooperation in manpower, logistics, training and defence hardware. On the topic of the regional situation, he expressed Pakistan’s commitment to constructive engagement with all parties to “build trust, bridge gaps and promote lasting peace, security and stability in the region”. During the meeting, Al Zayani conveyed the greetings of King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, the crown prince and prime minister of Bahrain, to the president, the statement added. He termed the JMC meetings “highly productive” and noted that the president’s visit to Bahrain had left “a significant and positive impact on bilateral relations”. He commended Pakistan’s courageous efforts to mediate amid the current regional situation and bring warring parties to the table, saying that Pakistan’s actions had “helped save many lives”. He appreciated Pakistan’s peace efforts and congratulated it on its successful tenure as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council. Meeting with PM Shehbaz The foreign minister also called on PM Shehbaz, who warmly welcomed him and conveyed his best wishes to the leadership and people of Bahrain, according to a press release by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). He reaffirmed Pakistan’s “deep appreciation for the longstanding and brotherly relations between Pakistan and Bahrain, founded on shared values, mutual trust, and close people-to-people ties”, the PMO said. PM Shehbaz expressed his satisfaction over the positive trajectory of bilateral relations. He emphasised Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening cooperation with Bahrain in diverse fields, “including trade, investment, energy, and human resource development”. FM Al-Zayani, meanwhile, conveyed the greetings and well-wishes of the leadership of Bahrain to the premier, and reaffirmed Bahrain’s commitment to further enhancing bilateral cooperation across mutually beneficial areas. “The two sides exchanged views on regional and international developments and emphasised the importance of continued consultations and coordination on issues of mutual interest,” the statement said. Al-Zayani “appreciated Pakistan’s constructive role and mediation efforts aimed at promoting peace and stability in the region”, the PMO added. The prime minister expressed confidence that the JMC session would provide “further impetus” to bilateral cooperation and help deepen the relationship between the two countries. “The meeting was held in a warm and cordial atmosphere, reflecting the close and longstanding fraternal ties between Pakistan and Bahrain,” the statement added. JMC meeting During the JMC meeting, Islamabad and Manama “agreed to deepen collaboration in trade and investment, energy, agriculture and food security, information technology, health, education and labour”, FO said. They also discussed measures to strengthen connectivity and promote people-to-people exchanges. Dar “underscored the importance of translating the longstanding and fraternal ties between Pakistan and Bahrain into tangible benefits for their people”. He further stressed effective implementation of the agreed outcomes through joint working groups, institutional partnerships and regular follow-up, FO added. The JMC was attended by high-level delegations from both sides. The Pakistani team included the secretaries of the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) and the Economic Affairs Division, along with the acting foreign secretary. The Bahraini side included senior officials and representatives of the Bahrain Chamber of Commerce and Industry. In his address to the JMC meeting, Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to increase bilateral trade with Bahrain to the $1 billion target set earlier . Noting the target of doubling trade in three years, of which one has already elapsed, Dar quipped, “But God forbid, if we miss [the target by] a few months, we have a great excuse that this period has been very turbulent.” Dar also referred to the potential Pakistan-GCC FTA, noting that the GCC secretary general told him the deal was “almost ripe”, with one country yet to give a green light to it. “I’m sure the signing of the free trade agreement between the GCC and Pakistan will surely help us in achieving our goals,” the deputy premier said, adding that it would lead to an increase in imports and exports. He requested the Bahraini side to work towards recognising degrees and professional qualifications, while facilitating greater mobility of skilled labour between the two countries. Bilateral meeting Prior to the Pakistan-Bahrain JMC, the two foreign ministers also held a separate meeting after Al Zayani’s arrival at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In a post on X about the “cordial” meeting, the Foreign Office (FO) said the two ministers “reviewed Pakistan–Bahrain relations and expressed satisfaction at the positive momentum in high-level engagement between the two countries”. “They discussed ways to further expand bilateral cooperation across areas of mutual interest, particularly in trade, economic and investment relations, as well as through engagement at multilateral fora.” The two sides also exchanged views on “regional and international developments of mutual interest and underscored that dialogue and diplomacy remain the most viable means of addressing challenges and resolving disputes”, FO added. According to an earlier FO statement, the two sides were to “review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and discuss ways to further strengthen cooperation across diverse areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, economic cooperation, defence and security, labour and manpower, and cultural exchanges”. “Pakistan and Bahrain enjoy close, brotherly relations founded on shared faith, common values, mutual respect, and longstanding people-to-people links,” FO noted. Dar and Al Zayani last met in September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where they discussed bilateral relations, including preparations for the JMC session. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments, with Al Zayani appreciating Pakistan’s constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability. Pak-Bahrain exchanges Islamabad and Manama had agreed to establish the JMC in 2014, when King Sheikh Hamad bin Isa bin Salman Al-Khalifa paid a three-day visit to Pakistan. Following the last JMC session in July 2021, which was held in Manama, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding to promote business between the two countries. Earlier this month, Dar chaired an inter-ministerial meeting to review preparations for the Pakistan-Bahrain JMC and directed the ministries concerned to pursue concrete outcomes from the Bahrain FM’s visit. The Pakistani leadership has also undertaken official visits to the Gulf kingdom in recent years. PM Shehbaz, accompanied by Dar, made a two-day trip to Bahrain in November 2025, during which he met with the king and crown prince there. Then, in January this year, President Zardari made a four-day trip to the kingdom, where he highlighted economic opportunities that Pakistan offers.

'Fake and fabricated': Info ministry rejects NYT report claiming PAF jets being used against Yemen's Houthis. The Ministry of Information dismissed on Thursday a news report claiming that Pakistan Air Force (PAF) aircraft were being used against the Yemen’s Houthis as “fake and fabricated”. A New York Times report published on Oct 7, a screenshot of which the ministry shared in an X post, cited an unnamed source as saying that PAF fighter jets were being employed against the group, amid the latter’s escalating conflict with Saudi Arabia. But the information ministry denied the report, saying in a post on X that the NYT story “attributing the employment of PAF aircraft against Houthis is fake and fabricated”. “International media houses are again asked to avoid speculative reporting with regards to employment of Pakistan’s military forces under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. “Details of any deployment, if necessary, will be given by the authorities concerned,” it added. Earlier this week, the ministry also termed a Reuters report claiming the deployment of 30,000 to 40,000 Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia as “speculative”. The development comes after Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance in Riyadh on Monday. The defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Monday’s meeting under the alliance was held to address the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia. A statement issued by the Foreign Office after the meeting said the member states had “decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats”. Separately, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and said Saudi Arabia had made “gains and recovered some areas” in Yemen in the ongoing fighting with the Houthis. Asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, the defence minister replied that both nations had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On Wednesday, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry also said Pakistani troops are in Saudi Arabia, adding that they had been in the kingdom “for decades” and across multiple domains. Escalating tensions The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Both sides have claimed strikes on each other as tensions remain high. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that they had struck the Saudi capital’s main international airport with a ballistic missile, in another attack on the kingdom claimed by the group. A day ago, Saudi authorities said three people were killed and 36 injured in attacks on two of the kingdom’s international airports including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs. For its part, a Saudi-led coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it “destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform” used in the attack on Riyadh. The Houthis, who control most of the country’s northwest, are battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and they captured swathes of coastal land. Yemen’s internationally recognised government this week declared a major counter-offensive and said Houthi fighters were pushed out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha. But the Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground. Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult. Meanwhile, Pakistan has expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On Sept 18, Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and defensive in nature.

How mutual funds play across market caps: From ICICI Bank and Reliance to PB Fintech and Ather Energy. Domestic mutual funds spread their investments across companies of different sizes, with each market-cap segment offering a distinct risk-return profile. Large-cap stocks typically provide greater stability and tend to be less volatile, making them a core component of many portfolios. Mid-caps offer a balance between relative stability and higher growth potential, while small- and micro-cap stocks can deliver stronger long-term gains but come with significantly greater volatility and downside risk. The mix varies depending on a fund’s mandate, valuations, economic conditions and the fund manager’s assessment of future opportunities. Holding stocks across market-cap segments can help funds capture growth opportunities while reducing their dependence on any single segment and moderating overall portfolio risk. Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. The New Forever War mloukili Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:38 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 1 minutes The New Forever War Originally published in Foreign Affairs Why America and Iran Fight On Without Victory Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Ali Vaez Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/AliVaez Related Tags Iran United States When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another. Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce. The full article can be read on the Foreign Affairs website.
